blocks.h: 1. (a) Why the Convention exists - the gap it closed

blocks.p: Before 1988 international law dealt with violence at sea principally through piracy, and the definition of piracy is narrow: it requires private ends, and it requires two ships. An attack mounted for political ends, by people who were already lawfully on board as passengers, is therefore not piracy at all. The seizure of the Achille Lauro in October 1985 demonstrated the consequence - a serious armed attack on a ship, with a passenger murdered, that fell outside the one offence the law of the sea universally recognised, leaving States arguing about who could prosecute.

blocks.h: 2. (a) The purpose of the Convention, and how it works

blocks.p: Its purpose is to ensure that appropriate action is taken against persons committing unlawful acts against the safety of maritime navigation, and it achieves this not by policing ships but by closing the jurisdictional gaps in which such offenders could shelter. The mechanism has three parts. It defines a set of offences and requires each State Party to make them punishable by appropriate penalties in its own law. It requires States Parties to establish jurisdiction over those offences on the familiar bases - flag, territory and nationality of the offender - and permits others. And it obliges a State Party in whose territory an alleged offender is found either to extradite him or to submit the case to its own competent authorities for prosecution - the aut dedere aut judicare obligation at Article 10. The offences are also treated as extraditable offences between Parties.

blocks.h: 3. (a) Its importance in enhancing maritime security

blocks.p: It matters for four reasons. It removes the safe haven - there is no longer a State in which such an offender can be found and simply released for want of jurisdiction. It reclassifies the conduct as crime rather than misfortune, which brings police, prosecutors and mutual legal assistance to bear instead of leaving it as a shipping matter. It reaches beyond piracy, covering political motive, insiders already lawfully on board, and attacks on navigational facilities ashore. And it completes the security architecture: the ISPS Code under SOLAS chapter XI-2 is preventive - security levels, ship and port facility security plans and officers, access control - while SUA is what happens after prevention fails. One keeps the attacker off the ship; the other ensures that if he gets on, he is tried.
Article 3 makes it an offence for any person unlawfully and intentionally to:

ol: seize or exercise control over a ship by force, threat of force or any other form of intimidation;
perform an act of violence against a person on board a ship, if it is likely to endanger the safe navigation of that ship;
destroy a ship, or cause damage to a ship or to its cargo, which is likely to endanger its safe navigation;
place, or cause to be placed, on a ship a device or substance likely to destroy or damage it;
destroy or seriously damage maritime navigational facilities, or seriously interfere with their operation, if likely to endanger safe navigation;
communicate information known to be false, thereby endangering safe navigation; and
injure or kill any person in connection with any of the above.

blocks.p: Attempt, abetting and threat are also covered. Note the recurring qualification - likely to endanger the safe navigation of the ship. That phrase is the boundary of the Convention: it is a navigation-safety instrument, not a general criminal code for the sea. A companion Protocol of the same date extends the scheme to fixed platforms on the continental shelf.

blocks.h: 5. (b) The new offences added by the 2005 Protocol

blocks.p: The 2005 Protocol was the response to 11 September 2001 and to concern about the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction. It inserts a substantial new body of offences, principally at Article 3bis, committed unlawfully and intentionally when the purpose is to intimidate a population or to compel a Government or an international organization to do or abstain from doing any act:

ul: using a ship itself as a weapon - using against or on a ship, or discharging from it, any explosive, radioactive material or biological, chemical or nuclear (BCN) weapon in a manner causing or likely to cause death, serious injury or damage;
discharging from a ship oil, liquefied natural gas or other hazardous or noxious substance in such quantity or concentration as to cause or be likely to cause death, serious injury or damage;
using a ship in a manner that causes death, serious injury or damage;

transporting on board a BCN weapon, or explosive or radioactive material, knowing it is intended for such use; and transporting dual-use equipment, materials, software or technology that significantly contributes to the design or manufacture of a BCN weapon, with intent that it be so used.

blocks.p: Article 3ter makes it an offence to transport a person known to have committed a SUA offence, intending to help him evade prosecution. Article 3quater deals with attempt, threat, participation, organising and directing, and contribution to a group acting with a common purpose.

blocks.h: 6. (b) The boarding regime - the enforcement half of the 2005 Protocol

blocks.p: New offences without a means of intercepting the ship would have been of limited value, so the Protocol adds a ship-boarding procedure at Article 8bis. Where a State Party has reasonable grounds to suspect that a ship is involved in a SUA offence, it may request the flag State's authorisation to board and search. The flag State may authorise, may board itself, may board jointly, or may decline. A State may also lodge a standing notification with the Secretary-General giving advance authorisation, or providing that authorisation is deemed granted if no response is received within four hours. Boarding is hedged with safeguards - the safety of life at sea, the security and commercial interests of the ship, humane treatment, and liability for damage where the suspicion proves unfounded. Critically, nothing displaces the primacy of the flag State: the Protocol creates a consent procedure, not a right of unilateral boarding.

blocks.h: 7. (b) How the amendments reflect evolving security concerns

blocks.p: The change is a change of fear. 1988 was written about hijacking - taking a ship and the people on it as leverage, so the harm contemplated was to the ship and to those on board, and every offence is tied to endangering safe navigation. 2005 was written about terrorism and proliferation, where the ship is not the target but the weapon or the delivery vehicle, and the harm contemplated is to a population ashore. Four shifts follow. The object of protection widens from the ship to the public. The ship becomes a means, not an end. Mere transport becomes criminal, which is a significant step - the offence is complete without any violence at all, and it makes SUA an instrument of non-proliferation alongside initiatives such as the Proliferation Security Initiative. And the treaty moves from prosecution to interdiction: 1988 dealt with offenders after the event, whereas Article 8bis is designed to stop the cargo before it arrives. The limits are equally revealing - boarding still depends on flag State consent, the offences still require a terrorist purpose, and the whole scheme still depends on each Party enacting and enforcing it domestically.

The marks are printed 6 and 10, and the split tells you where the writing goes. Limb (a) is worth 6 and asks two things - purpose and importance in enhancing maritime security. Limb (b) is worth 10 and asks two things - the main offences under the 1988 Convention and its 2005 Protocol, and how these amendments reflect evolving security concerns.

The commonest failure is to spend the whole answer listing offences and never reach the word reflect. That final analysis is worth several marks on its own and it is the only part of the question that asks the candidate to think rather than recall. Step 7 exists to guarantee it gets written.

blocks.h: The one idea that organises the whole question

blocks.p: SUA exists because piracy is defined too narrowly. Piracy needs private ends and two ships. The Achille Lauro attackers had political ends and were already on board as passengers - so on the law as it then stood, no piracy, and a serious argument about who could try them. Everything in this question descends from that single gap: the 1988 offences fill it, the jurisdiction and extradite-or-prosecute machinery makes it enforceable, and the 2005 Protocol widens it again when the threat changed shape.

For limb (b), hold the shift in one line: 1988 - the ship is the TARGET. 2005 - the ship is the WEAPON or the DELIVERY VEHICLE. Every one of the new offences and the boarding regime can be reasoned from that sentence.

blocks.h: The dates, which are the easy marks

ul: Achille Lauro seized October 1985 - the trigger.
SUA Convention adopted at Rome 10 March 1988, in force 1 March 1992. A companion Protocol of the same date covers fixed platforms on the continental shelf.
2005 Protocols adopted in London 14 October 2005, in force 28 July 2010.
Both are in force at the date of this paper by a wide margin - there is no adopted-but-not-in-force problem on this question, which is unusual and worth saying.
Treating SUA as an anti-piracy convention. It exists precisely because the conduct it covers is not piracy.
Confusing it with the ISPS Code. ISPS is preventive and sits under SOLAS chapter XI-2; SUA is criminal law and applies after the event.
Saying the Convention lets a warship board any suspect ship. Article 8bis is a flag State consent procedure, not a right of unilateral boarding.
Forgetting the qualifier 'likely to endanger the safe navigation of the ship' on the 1988 offences. It is the boundary of the whole instrument.
Listing the offences and never answering how the amendments reflect evolving security concerns.
Omitting the transport offences from 2005. They are the most significant single addition, because the offence is complete without any violence.
Inventing article numbers. Give the ones you are sure of and describe the rest.
Quoting a number of States Parties. It changes constantly and cannot be verified in an examination.
Why was SUA needed when piracy was already an international crime? Because piracy requires private ends and two ships. This is the discriminating answer.

Does SUA apply to a ship in port? The Convention is framed around navigation and applies where the ship is navigating or scheduled to navigate into, through or from waters beyond the territorial sea of a single State. Do not claim it covers every event on every ship everywhere.
Who prosecutes? Any State Party with jurisdiction; and the State where the offender is found must extradite or submit the case to its own authorities - Article 10.

Can I board a suspect ship on the high seas under SUA? Only with the flag State's authorisation, which may be given in advance or deemed after four hours if that State has so notified. The flag State's primacy is preserved.
What is the single biggest change made in 2005? Criminalising transport of BCN weapons and related dual-use material - the ship becomes a proliferation route, and no violence need occur.
Is SUA self-executing? No. Each State Party must make the offences punishable in its own law, which is where the practical weakness lies.
What incident led to the SUA Convention?
Why was that incident not piracy?
Name four offences under the 1988 Convention.
What does aut dedere aut judicare mean?
What did the 2005 Protocol add, and why?
What does BCN stand for?
As Master, a warship requests to board on suspicion of a SUA offence. What is the position?
How does SUA differ from the ISPS Code?
Is there a companion instrument for offshore installations?

blocks.p: Three blocks. (a) WHY, WHAT, WHY IT MATTERS - the piracy gap and Achille Lauro (1), purpose and the three-part mechanism (2), importance and the contrast with ISPS (3). (b) OFFENCES - 1988 (4), then 2005 new offences (5), then boarding (6). (b) ANALYSIS - the shift of fear (7).

For the 1988 offence list use SEIZE - VIOLENCE - DESTROY - PLACE - FACILITIES - FALSE INFORMATION - KILL, and remember that all of them hang on 'likely to endanger safe navigation'. For 2005 use USE - DISCHARGE - TRANSPORT - HARBOUR: use the ship as a weapon, discharge something lethal from it, transport a BCN weapon or dual-use material, or carry a fugitive offender.

blocks.p: This is the weakest evidence position on the paper and it is declared rather than concealed. The MIW True Source corpus holds neither the SUA Convention 1988 nor either of the 2005 Protocols. Every treaty statement above is therefore authoritative restatement, classified P2, not primary. No article is quoted anywhere.

Article identities are given only where the answer can carry them honestly - Article 3 for the 1988 offences, Articles 3bis, 3ter and 3quater for the 2005 additions, Article 8bis for boarding and Article 10 for prosecute-or-extradite. No other article number is asserted, and none has been invented to make the answer look better sourced than it is. Acquiring the consolidated 2005 texts would promote this whole answer to primary, and that is recorded as an acquisition need.

Two further omissions are deliberate. No number of States Parties, no tonnage coverage figure and no prosecution statistic is given - party counts move continuously and MIW holds no status list, so any figure stated as at November 2024 would be unverifiable. And no Indian implementing statute is named; the question does not ask for one, the corpus supports none, and inventing a statutory reference would be worse than omitting it.

On currency: this is one of the few questions on the paper with no 2024 boundary at all. Both instruments were in force long before the sitting - by thirty-two and fourteen years respectively - so there is nothing here that a later or earlier sitting would change. The answer is stable across sittings, which is itself worth knowing.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Why it exists. Piracy needs private ends and two ships, so the Achille Lauro attack of October 1985 - political motive, attackers already on board - was not piracy, and nobody was clearly entitled to prosecute. Instrument. SUA Convention, adopted Rome 10 March 1988, in force 1 March 1992; companion Protocol on fixed platforms. Purpose. Ensure appropriate action against unlawful acts against safe navigation, by closing jurisdictional gaps: define offences, require Parties to criminalise them, establish jurisdiction, and prosecute or extradite (Article 10). Importance. No safe haven; conduct becomes crime; reaches beyond piracy; and complements ISPS under SOLAS XI-2 - ISPS prevents, SUA punishes. 1988 offences (Article 3). SEIZE a ship by force; VIOLENCE against a person on board; DESTROY/DAMAGE ship or cargo; PLACE a device or substance; damage NAVIGATIONAL FACILITIES; FALSE INFORMATION; INJURE OR KILL in connection - all 'likely to endanger safe navigation'. 2005 Protocol, adopted 14 October 2005, in force 28 July 2010. Article 3bis - using the ship as a weapon; discharging explosive, radioactive material or a BCN weapon; discharging oil/LNG/HNS lethally; TRANSPORTING BCN weapons or dual-use material. 3ter - carrying a fugitive offender. 3quater - attempt, threat, participation. Article 8bis - boarding with FLAG STATE authorisation, advance consent or deemed after four hours, with safeguards. The shift. 1988 ship = TARGET; 2005 ship = WEAPON or DELIVERY VEHICLE - protection widens to the public, transport alone becomes criminal, and the treaty moves from prosecution to interdiction.

questions.understand_first: This question is really about a hole in the law and how it was patched twice. For centuries the only universally recognised crime at sea was piracy, and piracy is defined tightly: it must be for private ends, and it must involve two ships - one attacking the other. In 1985 a group of men who had boarded the Achille Lauro as ordinary passengers seized her for openly political ends and murdered a passenger. On the definition, that was not piracy. There was no second ship and no private end, and so there was no offence that every State was entitled to prosecute, and a genuine argument about jurisdiction followed. The SUA Convention is the patch: it does not try to police ships or prevent attacks - the ISPS Code does that - it simply creates the offences and makes sure somebody has to try them, wherever the offender turns up. Then the world's fear changed. After 2001 the worry was no longer that someone would take a ship hostage; it was that someone would use a ship - as a bomb, or as the quiet way to move a nuclear component across an ocean. So the 2005 Protocol patches the patch: new offences in which the ship is the weapon or the delivery vehicle, transport alone made criminal, and for the first time a procedure for stopping the ship before it arrives. Hold that arc - target becomes weapon, prosecution becomes interdiction - and the whole of limb (b) writes itself.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the SUA Convention question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb (a): 1 the gap - why it is not piracy, and the Achille Lauro. 2 purpose and the three-part mechanism. 3 importance, and the ISPS contrast. Limb (b): 4 the 1988 offences. 5 the 2005 new offences. 6 the Article 8bis boarding regime. 7 how the amendments reflect evolving security concerns.
retrieval_cards.why: The 6/10 split puts the weight in limb (b), and step 7 exists to guarantee the analytical demand is answered rather than crowded out by the offence list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why was the SUA Convention needed when piracy was already an international crime?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because piracy is defined too narrowly. It requires an act committed for private ends and it requires two ships - one attacking another. The Achille Lauro attackers acted for political ends and were already lawfully on board as passengers, so no piracy was committed and no State had clear universal jurisdiction. SUA creates offences that do not depend on motive or on a second ship.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most discriminating fact in the answer, and the reason the Convention exists at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the principal offences created by Article 3 of the 1988 Convention.
retrieval_cards.answer: Unlawfully and intentionally: seizing or exercising control over a ship by force, threat or intimidation; performing an act of violence against a person on board if likely to endanger safe navigation; destroying a ship or damaging it or its cargo so as to endanger safe navigation; placing on board a device or substance likely to destroy or damage it; destroying or seriously damaging maritime navigational facilities or seriously interfering with their operation; communicating information known to be false and thereby endangering safe navigation; and injuring or killing any person in connection with any of these. Attempt, abetting and threat are also covered.
retrieval_cards.why: Seven limbs, and they are countable marks. Note that almost every one is qualified by 'likely to endanger the safe navigation of the ship'.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does aut dedere aut judicare require, and where is it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Prosecute or extradite. Under Article 10, a State Party in whose territory an alleged offender is found must either extradite him or, without exception and without undue delay, submit the case to its own competent authorities for the purpose of prosecution. This is the mechanism that removes the safe haven, and it is what makes the Convention effective rather than declaratory.
retrieval_cards.why: The heart of the Convention's purpose limb, and a standard oral follow-up.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the SUA Convention differ from the ISPS Code?
retrieval_cards.answer: The ISPS Code, under SOLAS chapter XI-2, is a preventive regime: security levels, ship and port facility security plans, security officers, access control and assessments, aimed at stopping an attack happening. The SUA Convention is criminal law: it defines offences, requires States Parties to criminalise them, allocates jurisdiction and obliges prosecution or extradition after the event. One keeps the attacker off the ship; the other ensures that if he gets on, he is tried.
retrieval_cards.why: The two are constantly confused, and the contrast is worth marks in limb (a)'s importance demand.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What did the 2005 Protocol add by way of new offences?
retrieval_cards.answer: Principally at Article 3bis, offences committed unlawfully and intentionally where the purpose is to intimidate a population or compel a Government or international organisation: using a ship as a weapon or discharging from it any explosive, radioactive material or biological, chemical or nuclear weapon so as to cause death, serious injury or damage; discharging oil, LNG or other hazardous or noxious substance in lethal quantity; using the ship in a manner causing death or serious injury; and transporting a BCN weapon or explosive or radioactive material, or dual-use equipment, materials, software or technology contributing to a BCN weapon. Article 3ter criminalises transporting a person known to have committed a SUA offence, and Article 3quater covers attempt, threat, participation, organising and directing.
retrieval_cards.why: The transport offences are the most significant addition, because the offence is complete without any violence at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A warship signals your ship on the high seas and requests to board under SUA. What is the legal position?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under Article 8bis the requesting State must seek the authorisation of your flag State. The flag State may authorise the boarding, may board itself, may board jointly, or may refuse. It may also have notified the Secretary-General in advance that it gives standing authorisation, or that authorisation is deemed granted if it does not respond within four hours. Safeguards apply: safety of life at sea, the security and commercial interests of the ship, humane treatment, and liability for damage if the suspicion proves unfounded. There is no right of unilateral boarding - flag State primacy is preserved.
retrieval_cards.why: The practical question a Chief Engineer or Master could actually face, and the point on which candidates most often overstate the Convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In one sentence, how do the 2005 amendments reflect evolving security concerns?
retrieval_cards.answer: In 1988 the ship was the target and the fear was hijacking for leverage, so every offence is tied to endangering the safe navigation of that ship; by 2005 the fear was terrorism and proliferation, in which the ship is the weapon or the delivery vehicle and the intended victims are ashore - so the protected object widens from the ship to the population, mere transport of weapons or dual-use material becomes criminal without any violence, and the treaty moves from prosecuting after the event to interdicting before it.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the printed analytical demand in limb (b) and it is what most candidates never reach.

blocks.h: 1. (a) What the Convention is, and the failure it was written to cure

blocks.p: The International Convention on Salvage, 1989 was adopted in London on 28 April 1989 and entered into force on 14 July 1996, replacing the Brussels Convention of 1910. The 1910 regime rested on one commercial rule - no cure, no pay: a salvor who produced no useful result earned nothing, however hard or however skilfully he worked.

That rule failed in exactly the case where society most needed a salvor. When a laden tanker went ashore and broke up, as in the Torrey Canyon and Amoco Cadiz class of casualty, the ship and cargo were lost, so there was no salved fund and no reward - yet the salvor's presence might have prevented an enormous pollution incident. The economics therefore discouraged the professional salvor from attending the most environmentally dangerous casualties, and encouraged him to leave once the property looked unsavable. The 1989 Convention exists to correct that.
Four, and they should be stated as such:

ol: To provide uniform international rules on salvage operations, replacing the 1910 Convention.
To preserve the incentive to salve - the reward regime is retained, and enlarged, so that professional salvors remain available and equipped.

To make protection of the environment an object of salvage law in its own right, rather than an incidental benefit - both by making environmental effort a criterion of the reward and by creating a separate entitlement where no reward is earned.

To impose duties on the parties - the salvor to exercise due care and to prevent or minimise damage to the environment, and the owner and master to co-operate, to exercise the same care, and to accept redelivery.

blocks.p: Article 12 retains no cure, no pay as the general rule; Article 14 is the deliberate exception to it.

blocks.h: 3. (a) How it balances the interests of salvors and owners

blocks.p: The balance is struck by giving each side what it most needs and capping what it fears. The salvor gets a reward fixed on criteria that reward skill, risk, promptness and readiness - not merely outcome - so that maintaining expensive standing capability is economically rational; and he gets a safety net under Article 14 so that attending a dangerous, low-value casualty does not bankrupt him. The owner and his underwriters get certainty: the Article 13 reward can never exceed the salved value, so liability is bounded by what was actually saved; special compensation is measured on expenses rather than as a share of value, so it cannot become a windfall; it is payable only to the extent it exceeds the Article 13 reward, so the salvor cannot be paid twice; and a negligent salvor may be deprived of it. The Convention also leaves the parties free to contract, which is why Lloyd's Open Form remains the usual instrument - the Convention sets the floor, not the whole bargain.

blocks.h: 4. (b) Article 13 - the criteria for fixing the reward

blocks.p: Article 13 requires the reward to be fixed with a view to encouraging salvage operations, taking the following criteria into account without regard to the order in which they are presented:

ol: the salved value of the vessel and other property;
the skill and efforts of the salvors in preventing or minimising damage to the environment;
the measure of success obtained by the salvor;
the nature and degree of the danger;
the skill and efforts of the salvors in salving the vessel, other property and life;
the time used and the expenses and losses incurred by the salvors;
the risk of liability and other risks run by the salvors or their equipment;
the promptness of the services rendered;
the availability and use of vessels or other equipment intended for salvage operations; and
the state of readiness, efficiency and value of the salvor's equipment.

blocks.p: Two features carry marks. The list is not ranked - salved value is listed first but is not the dominant factor. And criterion two, environmental effort, sits inside the ordinary reward. That is the 1989 Convention's first environmental mechanism, and it is separate from and prior to Article 14: a salvor who protects the environment is paid more even where the salvage succeeds.

The reward is paid by the vessel and other property interests in proportion to their respective salved values - so ship and cargo contribute according to what each had saved. And the reward, exclusive of interest and recoverable legal costs, shall not exceed the salved value of the vessel and other property. That cap is the owner's and the underwriter's protection, and it is precisely why Article 14 had to be created: where salved value is nil or trivial, a cap expressed as a proportion of it is worth nothing.

Article 14 applies where the salvor has carried out operations in respect of a vessel which by itself or its cargo threatened damage to the environment and has failed to earn a reward under Article 13 at least equivalent to the special compensation assessable. He is then entitled to special compensation from the owner of the vessel, equivalent to his expenses.

ul: The uplift. If the salvor has by his operations actually prevented or minimised damage to the environment, the special compensation may be increased by up to 30 per cent of his expenses; and a tribunal, if it thinks it fair and just, may increase it further - but never beyond 100 per cent of the expenses incurred.
What expenses means. The out-of-pocket expenses reasonably incurred in the operation, plus a fair rate for equipment and personnel actually and reasonably used.
The offset. Special compensation is payable only if, and to the extent that, it exceeds any reward recoverable under Article 13. It is a safety net, not a second payment.
Forfeiture. The salvor may be deprived of the whole or part of it if he was negligent and has thereby failed to prevent or minimise damage to the environment.

blocks.p: Note who pays. The Article 13 reward comes from ship and cargo in proportion to salved values; special compensation comes from the shipowner alone - which in practice means his P&I club, whereas the reward falls largely on hull and cargo underwriters.

blocks.h: 7. (b) Why the two articles matter together

blocks.p: Their significance is that together they made environmental protection commercially rational. Article 13 pays a salvor more for protecting the environment when he succeeds; Article 14 pays him something for trying when he fails. The gap between them - the case of the dangerous, low-value wreck - was exactly the gap that had kept salvors away. The Convention thereby converted an environmental duty into an economic incentive without abandoning no cure, no pay as the general rule.

The practical sequel is worth a line. Article 14's fair rate was construed as covering expenses without any profit element, which made the entitlement unattractive and made every claim a lengthy argument about what had been spent. The industry's answer was contractual, not legislative: the SCOPIC clause, incorporated into Lloyd's Open Form, which substitutes an agreed tariff for the Article 14 assessment and can be invoked by the salvor regardless of environmental threat, with the shipowner providing security. SCOPIC is a contractual mechanism and forms no part of the Convention - but it is the reason Article 14 rarely has to be assessed in practice today.

The marks are printed 6 and 10. Limb (a) asks two things - the primary objectives, and how the Convention balances the interests of salvors and vessel owners. Limb (b) asks three - the significance of Articles 13 and 14, the criteria for determining the reward under Article 13, and the provisions of Article 14 on special compensation.

The word significance is doing real work and it is routinely ignored. It is not asking what the articles say - the rest of the limb asks that. It is asking why they matter, which means why the two together changed the economics of salvage. Step 7 exists so that demand is answered.

blocks.h: The one idea that organises the whole question

blocks.p: No cure, no pay fails exactly where the environment needs a salvor most. Under the 1910 regime, a salvor was paid out of what he saved. If the tanker broke up and the cargo was lost, there was nothing saved, so there was nothing to pay him from - even if his presence had prevented a far worse spill. The rational salvor therefore stayed away from the most dangerous casualties, or left once the property looked unsavable.

Everything in the 1989 Convention follows from fixing that. Article 13 pays you more for protecting the environment when you succeed. Article 14 pays you something for trying when you fail. If you can write those two sentences you can reconstruct the rest of the answer.

blocks.h: Get the two articles apart - the commonest confusion on this question

blocks.p: If you remember only one row, remember who pays. The reward comes out of the salved property; special compensation comes out of the shipowner's pocket. That single distinction explains why the two are argued about so fiercely and why SCOPIC exists.

blocks.h: The numbers that must be exact

ul: Adopted 28 April 1989, in force 14 July 1996, replacing the 1910 Brussels Convention.
Ten criteria in Article 13, taken without regard to the order in which they are presented.
The Article 13 reward shall not exceed the salved value of vessel and other property.
Article 14 uplift: up to 30 per cent of expenses where environmental damage was prevented or minimised; a tribunal may go further but never beyond 100 per cent.
Expenses = out-of-pocket expenses reasonably incurred plus a fair rate for equipment and personnel actually and reasonably used.
Saying the 1989 Convention abolished no cure, no pay. It did not. Article 12 keeps it as the general rule; Article 14 is a defined exception.
Treating Article 14 as an addition to the Article 13 reward. It is payable only to the extent it exceeds the reward.

Forgetting that environmental effort is already a criterion under Article 13. Candidates routinely present Article 13 as purely commercial and Article 14 as the only green provision. It is the second criterion in the list.
Giving the 30 per cent as the absolute maximum. The tribunal may go beyond it, up to 100 per cent of expenses.
Saying special compensation is paid by ship and cargo. It is paid by the owner of the vessel.
Presenting SCOPIC as part of the Convention. It is a clause in Lloyd's Open Form - industry contract, not treaty.
Ranking the Article 13 criteria, or saying salved value is the dominant one. The article says the criteria are taken without regard to their order.
Quoting an award figure or a percentage of salved value from a decided case. Awards are fact-specific.
Did 1989 end no cure, no pay? No - it created a bounded exception for environmental cases.
Which article protects the environment? Both. Article 13 through the second criterion; Article 14 through the separate entitlement. Answering 'Article 14' alone is a half mark.
Who pays special compensation, and which insurer? The shipowner, and in practice his P&I club - not the hull and cargo underwriters who fund the reward.
What is the maximum special compensation? Expenses plus an uplift of up to 30 per cent, which a tribunal may increase but never beyond 100 per cent of expenses.

Why was SCOPIC needed if Article 14 existed? Because 'fair rate' was construed as expenses without a profit element, so the entitlement was unattractive and every claim became an argument about quantum.
Can a salvor lose special compensation? Yes - he may be deprived of all or part of it if his negligence has failed to prevent or minimise environmental damage.
Does the reward have a ceiling? Yes - the salved value of the vessel and other property. That ceiling is why Article 14 had to exist at all.

blocks.p: Two limbs, seven steps. Limb (a) - THE FAILURE (1), the objectives (2), the balance (3). Limb (b) - CRITERIA (4), the cap (5), SPECIAL COMPENSATION (6), and why the two matter together (7).

For the ten Article 13 criteria, group them in three: WHAT WAS AT STAKE - salved value, environmental effort, measure of success, nature and degree of danger. WHAT THE SALVOR PUT IN - skill and efforts, time and expenses, risk run, promptness. WHAT HE HAD READY - availability and use of salvage craft, and the state, efficiency and value of his equipment. Four, four, two.
For Article 14 use E-30-100: Expenses, uplift up to 30 per cent, tribunal may go to 100 per cent, never beyond.

blocks.p: The MIW True Source corpus does not hold the International Convention on Salvage, 1989. Every treaty statement above is therefore authoritative restatement, classified P2, not primary, and no article is quoted anywhere. quick_revision.recall_15s: Instrument. International Convention on Salvage, adopted London 28 April 1989, in force 14 July 1996, replacing the 1910 Brussels Convention. The failure it cured. Under no cure, no pay a salvor was paid out of what he saved - so where the tanker broke up there was no fund and no reward, and salvors stayed away from the most environmentally dangerous casualties. Objectives. Uniform rules; preserve the incentive to salve; make environmental protection an object of salvage law; impose duties on salvor, owner and master. Article 12 keeps no cure, no pay; Article 14 is the exception. Balance. Salvor gets reward for skill, risk, promptness, readiness, plus a safety net; owner gets a cap at salved value, a compensation measured on expenses not value, an offset so no double payment, and forfeiture for a negligent salvor. Article 13 - TEN criteria, unranked: salved value; skill and efforts in preventing or minimising environmental damage; measure of success; nature and degree of danger; skill and efforts in salving; time, expenses and losses; risk of liability; promptness; availability and use of salvage craft; state of readiness, efficiency and value of equipment. Paid by ship and cargo in proportion to salved values; shall not exceed the salved value. Article 14 - special compensation. Trigger: vessel or cargo threatened damage to the environment and the reward is less than the compensation assessable. Paid by the SHIPOWNER alone, equal to expenses; uplift up to 30 per cent if damage actually prevented or minimised; tribunal may go further but never beyond 100 per cent. Expenses = out-of-pocket plus a fair rate for equipment and personnel actually and reasonably used. Payable only to the extent it exceeds the Article 13 reward; forfeitable for negligence. Significance. 13 pays you more for succeeding greenly; 14 pays you something for trying. 'Fair rate' meant expenses without profit, so the industry wrote SCOPIC into LOF - contract, not treaty.
critical_numbers: Adopted London 28 April 1989; entered into force 14 July 1996; replaced the Brussels Convention of 1910
Article 13 lists TEN criteria, taken without regard to the order in which they are presented
The Article 13 reward shall NOT EXCEED the salved value of the vessel and other property
Article 14 uplift: up to 30 per cent of expenses where environmental damage was prevented or minimised
A tribunal may increase it further if fair and just, but NEVER BEYOND 100 PER CENT of the expenses incurred
Special compensation is payable only if, and to the extent that, it EXCEEDS the Article 13 reward
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Articles 13 and 14 of the International Convention on Salvage, 1989. Article 13 fixes the reward on ten unranked criteria - the second of which is the salvor's skill and efforts in preventing or minimising damage to the environment - paid by ship and cargo in proportion to salved values and capped at the salved value. Article 14 gives special compensation from the shipowner alone, measured on expenses, with an uplift of up to 30 per cent and a tribunal discretion never exceeding 100 per cent, payable only to the extent it exceeds the reward. MIW holds no copy of the Convention; both are cited by identity and nothing is quoted.
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying the 1989 Convention abolished no cure, no pay. It did not - Article 12 retains it and Article 14 is a bounded exception. The second trap is treating special compensation as an addition to the reward; it is payable only to the extent it exceeds it. The third is presenting Article 14 as the only environmental provision: environmental effort is already the second of the ten Article 13 criteria. The fourth is giving 30 per cent as the absolute maximum - a tribunal may go beyond it, up to 100 per cent of expenses.

questions.memory_cue: Two limbs, seven steps. Limb (a) - the commercial failure (1), the four objectives (2), the balance from both sides (3). Limb (b) - the ten criteria (4), apportionment and the cap (5), special compensation (6), and why the pair matters (7). For the ten criteria count four, four, two: what was at stake, what the salvor put in, what he had ready. For Article 14 use E-30-100: Expenses, 30 per cent uplift, tribunal to 100 per cent, never beyond.
questions.understand_first: Salvage law has always run on a single hard bargain: no cure, no pay. Save the property and you get a reward out of it; save nothing and you get nothing, however heroic the attempt. That bargain worked for centuries because the only thing at risk was property. Then tankers got large. When a laden tanker goes ashore, the thing society most wants is a professional salvor alongside her fast - but that is precisely the case where the ship and her cargo are most likely to be a total loss, and under the old rule a total loss meant no salved fund and therefore no reward at all. So the law was paying salvors to attend the casualties that mattered least and paying them nothing to attend the ones that mattered most. The 1989 Convention is the fix, and it works on two levels, which is why the examiner named two articles. Article 13 keeps the reward but changes what it is calculated on - it adds the salvor's environmental effort to the list of things he is paid for, so protecting the coast makes him more money when he succeeds. Article 14 adds a floor - if there was an environmental threat and the reward comes to less than his costs, the shipowner must cover his expenses anyway, with a bonus if he actually prevented damage. One rewards success, the other underwrites the attempt. Hold that and the numbers, the caps and even SCOPIC all follow.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the Salvage Convention question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb (a): 1 the commercial failure of no cure, no pay. 2 the four primary objectives. 3 how the interests are balanced. Limb (b): 4 the ten Article 13 criteria. 5 apportionment and the salved-value cap. 6 Article 14 special compensation. 7 why the two articles matter together.
retrieval_cards.why: The printed word 'significance' in limb (b) is answered by step 7, and it is the demand candidates most often crowd out with description.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Did the 1989 Convention abolish no cure, no pay?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Article 12 retains it as the general rule - salvage operations which have had a useful result give a right to a reward, and no payment is due if they have had no useful result. Article 14 is a bounded exception for cases where the vessel or its cargo threatened damage to the environment. The Convention modified the bargain; it did not abandon it.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most common error on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the criteria for fixing a salvage reward under Article 13.
retrieval_cards.answer: Ten, taken without regard to the order in which they are presented: the salved value of the vessel and other property; the skill and efforts of the salvors in preventing or minimising damage to the environment; the measure of success obtained; the nature and degree of the danger; the skill and efforts in salving the vessel, other property and life; the time used and the expenses and losses incurred; the risk of liability and other risks run; the promptness of the services; the availability and use of vessels or other equipment intended for salvage; and the state of readiness, efficiency and value of the salvor's equipment.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner named the article, so a partial list reads as partial knowledge. Note that the criteria are expressly unranked.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the ceiling on an Article 13 reward, and who pays it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The reward, exclusive of interest and recoverable legal costs, shall not exceed the salved value of the vessel and other property. It is paid by the vessel and the other property interests in proportion to their respective salved values, so ship and cargo each contribute according to what was saved for them. That ceiling is the owner's and underwriter's protection - and it is exactly why Article 14 was necessary, because a cap expressed as a share of a nil salved value is worth nothing.
retrieval_cards.why: The cap is the hinge between the two articles; explaining it is what makes the Article 14 answer coherent.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the provisions of Article 14 on special compensation.
retrieval_cards.answer: Where the salvor has worked on a vessel which by itself or its cargo threatened damage to the environment and has failed to earn a reward at least equivalent to the special compensation assessable, he is entitled to special compensation from the owner of the vessel equal to his expenses. If he actually prevented or minimised damage to the environment it may be increased by up to 30 per cent of those expenses, and a tribunal may go further if fair and just but never beyond 100 per cent. Expenses means out-of-pocket costs reasonably incurred plus a fair rate for equipment and personnel actually and reasonably used. It is payable only to the extent it exceeds the Article 13 reward, and may be forfeited in whole or part for salvor negligence.
retrieval_cards.why: Six components. The two percentages and the offset are the marks most often lost.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who pays the reward, and who pays special compensation - and which insurer bears each?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Article 13 reward is paid by the vessel and the other property interests in proportion to their salved values, so it falls in practice on hull and cargo underwriters. Special compensation under Article 14 is paid by the owner of the vessel alone, and falls in practice on his P&I club. It is not shared with cargo.
retrieval_cards.why: The distinction that explains why the two articles are argued over so fiercely, and why SCOPIC security is a P&I matter.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which article of the Convention protects the environment?
retrieval_cards.answer: Both. Article 13 does it inside the ordinary reward, because the salvor's skill and efforts in preventing or minimising damage to the environment is the second of the ten criteria - so environmental effort increases the reward even where the salvage succeeds. Article 14 does it by creating a separate entitlement where no adequate reward is earned. Answering Article 14 alone misses half of the Convention's environmental mechanism.
retrieval_cards.why: A very common half-answer, and the examiner's natural probe on a question that names both articles.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are LOF and SCOPIC, and what is their relationship to the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Lloyd's Open Form is the standard no-cure-no-pay salvage contract under which the Convention regime is most often operated. SCOPIC is a clause incorporated into it which replaces the Article 14 assessment with an agreed tariff, can be invoked by the salvor regardless of environmental threat, and is secured by the shipowner. Both are industry contract and form no part of the Convention. SCOPIC exists because the Article 14 'fair rate' was construed as covering expenses without a profit element, which made the statutory entitlement unattractive and every claim an argument about quantum.
retrieval_cards.why: Explains the practical significance of Article 14, but must be labelled as contract - presenting SCOPIC as treaty is a clear error.

cross_links.label: QP2411 Q5 - the salvage regime whose reward falls on hull and cargo and whose special compensation falls on the P&I club

blocks.h: 1. (a) What hull and machinery insurance is

blocks.p: H&M is insurance of the ship herself. It is a property cover: it indemnifies the owner for physical loss of or damage to the hull, machinery, equipment and fittings, and for certain associated liabilities. It is placed in the commercial market - Lloyd's, company underwriters or the Nordic market - for a fixed premium, usually for a twelve-month period, on an agreed value, and subject to a deductible below which the owner carries the loss himself.

It is written on standard market forms rather than bespoke wordings - principally the Institute Time Clauses - Hulls, the International Hull Clauses or the Nordic Marine Insurance Plan. The insurer is a commercial insurer writing for profit, and the relationship is an ordinary contract of indemnity.
P&I is insurance of the owner's legal liabilities to third parties arising out of the operation of the ship. It is not property insurance at all: it responds to what the owner must pay somebody else.

Its structure is quite different. It is written by mutual associations - P&I clubs - which the shipowners themselves own. There are no external shareholders and no profit motive; each member is simultaneously insurer and assured. Members contribute by calls rather than premium: an advance call at the start of the policy year, a supplementary call if the year's claims exceed expectation, and in an extreme year an overspill call. Cover is defined by the club rules, which the members make, and the Board retains a discretion to meet claims that fall outside them.

Most of the world fleet is entered with clubs in the International Group, which allows the mutual system to carry catastrophic exposure: each club retains claims up to its own retention, claims above that are pooled and shared among the Group clubs, above the pool sits a collective market reinsurance programme, and above that an overspill arrangement. That structure is why a single mutual can stand behind a liability far larger than any one club.

blocks.p: The single sentence that carries the distinction: H&M answers the question 'what has happened to my ship?'; P&I answers the question 'what do I now owe to somebody else?'

The governing law, which both covers sit inside. This is an Indian examination and the operative statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. It is modelled on the United Kingdom Marine Insurance Act 1906 but it is the 1963 Act that governs, and it supplies the general law of the contract within which both covers operate - insurable interest, the duty of utmost good faith (section 19) and the consequent duty of disclosure (section 20), warranties, the classification of losses, and general average loss (section 66). Two cautions follow. The UK Insurance Act 2015 reform of the avoidance remedy is not part of Indian law and must not be imported. And the statute governs the contract of marine insurance; a P&I club entry is a mutual arrangement governed by the club's own rules, which is one more reason the two covers are not simply two policies of the same kind.

Because neither covers the other's field, and each exposure alone can destroy the business. Without H&M, a total loss destroys the asset - and with it the security on which the ship was financed, which is why mortgagees require it as a condition of lending. Without P&I, a single incident can produce liabilities that are not bounded by the ship's value at all: a serious pollution incident, a passenger casualty or a large cargo claim can exceed the vessel's worth many times over, and no property policy would respond to a penny of it.

There is also a hard practical reason. Compulsory insurance certification under the liability conventions is supported by the club, so a ship that is not entered in an acceptable P&I club cannot obtain the certificates it needs and will not be permitted to trade. In practice, entry is a condition of trading, and hull cover is a condition of financing.

blocks.h: 5. (b) Typical risks covered by H&M, and when it responds

blocks.p: The hull policy covers physical damage to and loss of the ship, from the traditional maritime perils and from a set of specified additional causes:

ul: Perils of the seas, fire and explosion, violent theft, jettison, piracy, and contact with aircraft, dock or harbour installations.

Under the Inchmaree or negligence clause, and subject to due diligence by the assured: bursting of boilers, breakage of shafts, latent defect in machinery or hull, and the negligence of master, officers, crew, pilots and repairers.
Total loss, actual or constructive, and particular average - partial damage.
The ship's contribution to general average and to salvage.
Sue and labour - the reasonable cost of steps taken to avert or minimise a covered loss.
Collision liability to another ship, traditionally three-fourths of it under the running-down clause.

blocks.p: Incidents where H&M responds. A main engine crankshaft fractures at sea and the engine is destroyed - hull, under the negligence and latent-defect cover, subject to due diligence and the deductible. The ship grounds and bottom plating is set up - hull, particular average. An engine-room fire gutters the machinery space - hull. The ship is a constructive total loss after grounding - hull pays the agreed value. In each case note what is being repaired: the owner's own property.

blocks.h: 6. (b) Typical risks covered by P&I, and when it responds

blocks.p: The club covers the owner's liabilities, costs and expenses to others:

ul: Crew - illness, injury and death, hospital and repatriation costs, wages during incapacity, and the cost of substitutes.
Passengers and other persons - injury, death and loss of effects.
Cargo - loss of, damage to and shortage of cargo carried.
Pollution - liability for oil and other pollution, clean-up costs and the resulting claims. This is the one major head that carries a specific monetary limit rather than the general unlimited cover.
Wreck removal where it is compulsorily required.
Damage to fixed and floating objects - berths, buoys, cables, cranes.
The collision liability not covered by the hull policy - the remaining fourth and any excess above the hull limit.
Fines, quarantine and diversion expenses, stowaways, life salvage, towage and contractual liabilities, and legal costs.

blocks.p: Incidents where P&I responds. A bunker overflow oils a berth and the harbour - club, for the clean-up and the third-party claims. An oiler is injured by a falling grating and repatriated - club. A reefer container's cargo is condemned on discharge - club. The ship strikes and demolishes a berth crane - club, as damage to a fixed object. The ship is arrested and the crew must be maintained and repatriated - club. In each case note who is being paid: somebody other than the owner.

blocks.h: 7. (b) The boundary - where both are engaged at once

blocks.p: The two covers meet in the same casualty more often than a table suggests, and this is where marks are won.

Collision. One event produces two quite different losses. Damage to your own ship is a hull claim. Liability to the other ship and her cargo is a liability claim, and it is split: the hull policy has traditionally taken three-fourths under the running-down clause and the club the remaining fourth and anything above the hull limit - though modern forms may write collision liability at four-fourths by agreement. If the collision also spills oil, the pollution liability is entirely the club's. So a single collision can involve the hull underwriter twice and the club twice, which is precisely why both must be placed with the casualty in mind.

General average. When the master makes a voluntary and extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure for the common safety - beaching a burning ship, engaging salvors, putting into a port of refuge - the loss is shared between ship, cargo and freight in proportion to value. The ship's contribution is a hull claim. The club's involvement is in the liability consequences, and in the salvage context it is the club that meets special compensation, where the reward itself falls on the salved property.

blocks.h: 8. (b) Their roles in managing liabilities and operational risk

blocks.p: They do different jobs and the difference is not only which cheque is written.

H&M manages capital risk. It converts an unpredictable catastrophic loss of the asset into a predictable annual premium, protects the mortgagee's security, and keeps a repair the owner cannot fund from becoming an insolvency. Its discipline runs through the deductible - the owner keeps small damage, so the incentive to maintain remains with him - and through warranties and class, since cover assumes the ship is in class and properly manned.

P&I manages liability risk, and it does far more than pay. Because the members own it, the club is also a service organisation: it appoints correspondents in every port, instructs lawyers and surveyors, provides security to lift an arrest, supports the compulsory-insurance certification without which the ship cannot trade, and issues loss-prevention guidance drawn from the whole fleet's claims. Its discipline runs through underwriting the member rather than the risk - a poorly managed owner meets rising calls, or is refused entry - and through the pay-to-be-paid principle, under which the member must generally discharge the liability before he is indemnified.

Read together, they cover the two ways a shipping company fails: it loses its ship, or it owes more than it is worth. H&M answers the first; P&I answers the second. Neither is a substitute for the other, and a responsible owner supplements both - with war risks, loss of hire and charterers' liability cover - according to the trade.

The marks are printed 8 and 8 - an even split, which is unusual and tells you the two limbs are equally weighted. Limb (a) asks three things: define both covers, outline the main differences in coverage and purpose, and say why both are essential. Limb (b) asks three: the typical risks covered by each, examples of incidents where each would respond, and their roles in managing liabilities and operational risks.

The word examples is printed and it is the cheapest set of marks on the question. Two or three concrete incidents per cover - a crankshaft failure, a bunker spill, an injured oiler, a demolished berth crane - are worth more than another paragraph of definition, and most candidates never write them.

blocks.h: The one sentence that carries the whole question

blocks.p: H&M answers 'what has happened to my ship?'. P&I answers 'what do I now owe to somebody else?'

Every difference in the table is a consequence of that. Because H&M insures a thing, it can be valued, so it has an agreed value and a limit. Because P&I insures a liability, it cannot be valued in advance, so the cover is effectively unlimited and had to be organised mutually - no commercial insurer would write unlimited liability for a profit margin. And because the members own the club, it behaves like a service organisation rather than a counterparty.

ul: Citing the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906 in an Indian examination. The operative statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963; the 1906 Act is its model, not the law here. The UK Insurance Act 2015 reform of the avoidance remedy does not apply either.
Saying P&I covers damage to the ship. It does not. That is the whole point of the distinction.
Saying H&M covers pollution. It does not. Pollution liability is a club matter throughout.
Calling a P&I contribution a premium. It is a call - and the difference matters, because a supplementary call can be levied after the event.
Describing a club as an insurance company. It is a mutual association owned by its members, who are both insurer and assured.
Getting the collision split backwards. The hull policy has traditionally taken three-fourths of the collision liability; the club takes the remaining fourth and any excess.
Forgetting that a collision produces two kinds of claim - damage to your own ship, and liability to theirs.
Answering limb (b) with more definitions and no incidents. The stem asks for examples.
Quoting monetary limits - the oil-pollution limit, club retentions, pooling layers. They are reset annually and cannot be verified in an examination.
Omitting the service role of the club - correspondents, security to lift an arrest, certification support, loss prevention. It is half of why P&I matters.
Which statute governs a contract of marine insurance here? The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 - not the UK 1906 Act. Utmost good faith at s.19, disclosure at s.20, general average loss at s.66.

Your ship spills oil in a collision. Who pays what? Damage to your own ship - hull. Liability to the other ship - three-fourths hull, one-fourth club, plus any excess. Pollution - entirely the club. This one question tests the whole answer.
Is P&I cover unlimited? Effectively yes for most heads, but not for oil pollution, which carries a specific cap. Say that without inventing the figure.
Why is P&I mutual and H&M commercial? Because an unquantifiable liability cannot be profitably underwritten at a fixed premium, whereas a ship has a value.

What is the Inchmaree clause? The negligence clause extending hull cover to bursting of boilers, breakage of shafts, latent defect and the negligence of crew, pilots and repairers - subject to due diligence by the assured.
What is 'pay to be paid'? The member must generally discharge the liability himself before the club indemnifies him.
Could you trade without P&I? In practice no - the certification for compulsory insurance under the liability conventions is supported by the club.
Who insists on hull cover? The mortgagee. It is the security for the loan.
What is a supplementary call? An additional contribution levied when the policy year's claims exceed what the advance calls raised - a feature no commercial policy has.
Define P&I in one sentence.
Name six heads of P&I cover.
What does the hull policy cover that a candidate would not expect? Latent defect and crew negligence, under the Inchmaree clause.
What is a deductible, and why does it exist?
What is the International Group, and why does it exist?
Your engine fails from a latent defect. Which policy, and what must you show? Hull, and due diligence.
A stevedore is injured by your crane. Which policy?
What is sue and labour?
Which insurance covers loss of earnings while the ship is repaired? Neither - that is loss of hire, a separate cover.
Which Act governs marine insurance in India, and what does section 19 provide?

blocks.p: Two limbs, eight steps, and one axis. Limb (a) - define HULL (1), define CLUB (2), tabulate the differences (3), say why both (4). Limb (b) - hull risks and incidents (5), club risks and incidents (6), the BOUNDARY (7), and the two kinds of risk management (8).

For the seven rows of the comparison, walk one question down the table: what, whose loss, who writes it, what is paid in, on what terms, how much, and why. For P&I heads of cover walk the ship from the inside out: CREW, PASSENGERS, CARGO, POLLUTION, WRECK, FIXED OBJECTS, COLLISION EXCESS, FINES AND COSTS - people first, then what you carry, then what you damage outside the ship.

blocks.p: This question has no governing instrument, and the answer does not invent one. Marine insurance is a matter of contract and market practice, not of IMO regulation. MIW holds no policy wording, no set of Institute or International Hull Clauses, no club rule book and no International Group pooling agreement - and these are commercial documents rather than public instruments, so this is not a gap that ordinary corpus acquisition closes. Every statement about cover is therefore industry practice or authoritative restatement, classified P2 or P3, never primary. No clause is quoted and no clause number is asserted anywhere.

No monetary figure of any kind appears in this answer, and that is deliberate rather than an omission. There is no oil-pollution limit, no passenger or crew limit, no club retention, no pooling layer, no reinsurance or overspill figure, no premium or call rate, no deductible and no claims statistic. The International Group's limits and layers are reset annually at renewal; MIW holds no source for them; and a figure given as at November 2024 could not be verified. The structure is described instead - retention, pool, market reinsurance, overspill - which is what the examiner is actually testing. No edition year is given for any clause set, for the same reason.

One point is stated with its variation rather than flattened. The three-fourths collision proportion under the running-down clause is the settled market convention and is what an examiner expects, but modern hull forms may write collision liability at four-fourths by agreement. Which applies in a given case depends on the actual policy, and the answer says so rather than presenting the traditional split as invariable.

On currency: this is one of the few questions on the paper with no 2024 boundary at all. Nothing in the structure of hull or P&I cover moved during 2024. The only moving parts are the annual limits and layers, which is exactly why none is quoted.

notes: NO INSTRUMENT AND THEREFORE NO INSTRUMENT BOUNDARY. Marine insurance is contract and market practice, not IMO regulation. There is no adoption, approval or entry-into-force date to place, and the answer states that absence rather than naming an instrument to sound authoritative.

NO 2024 MOVEMENT. Nothing in the structure of hull and machinery cover or of P&I cover changed during 2024. The distinction, the mutual structure, the International Group architecture and the collision split are all long settled.

THE ONLY MOVING PARTS ARE ANNUAL, AND NONE IS QUOTED. International Group limits, club retentions, pooling layers, reinsurance limits and call rates are reset at each renewal. decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two printed limbs at 8 and 8 - an even split, so neither limb may be treated as the minor one. Limb (a) is definitional and comparative: DEFINE both covers, OUTLINE THE MAIN DIFFERENCES in coverage and purpose, and explain WHY BOTH ARE ESSENTIAL to shipowners. Limb (b) is applied: the TYPICAL RISKS covered by each, EXAMPLES OF INCIDENTS where each would respond, and their ROLES IN MANAGING LIABILITIES AND OPERATIONAL RISKS. The printed word 'examples' is an explicit instruction and is the cheapest mark on the question.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 8 + 8 printed. In limb (a), roughly two marks for each definition, two for the comparison and two for the case for both. In limb (b), roughly two and a half marks for each cover's risks and incidents, and three for the risk-management analysis. The even split means an answer that writes six paragraphs of definition and two lines of application loses half the question.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That a management-level candidate knows H&M insures the ship and P&I insures liability to others; knows P&I is MUTUAL and funded by calls rather than premium, and can say why that structure exists; can list the principal heads of each cover; can give concrete incidents rather than categories; knows the collision liability split and that pollution is entirely a club matter; and understands that the club is a service organisation - correspondents, security, certification support, loss prevention - and not merely a payer.

decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW on structure, which has been settled for many decades and did not move in 2024. The genuine exposure is NUMERICAL rather than structural: International Group limits, club retentions, pooling layers, reinsurance limits and call rates are reset at every renewal, so any figure would be stale or unverifiable. Controlled absolutely - no monetary figure of any kind appears anywhere in the answer.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW - the question is commercial and international and asks for no statutory limb. No Indian provision is asserted. Note that a candidate revising in 2026 might reach for the Merchant Shipping Act 2025, which did not commence until 15 March 2026 and must not appear.
technical_ambiguities: 'Define P&I insurance and H&M insurance' invites two textbook sentences and nothing more. The definitions are written so that the STRUCTURAL difference - commercial indemnity against mutual liability cover - is visible in the definition itself, because that is what generates the rest of the comparison.

'Why are both types of insurance essential' can be answered as a truism. It is answered concretely instead: without hull there is no security for the mortgage, and without club entry the ship cannot obtain compulsory-insurance certification and cannot trade.

The collision liability split is usually taught as an invariable three-fourths. It is the settled convention but modern hull forms may write four-fourths by agreement, and the answer states the variation rather than flattening it.

General average is not mentioned in the stem and could be treated as out of scope. It appears once, at the boundary step, because it is the clearest case where a hull claim and a liability exposure arise from the same act - but it is not allowed to take over an answer about two classes of insurance.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Four steps for limb (a): define each cover separately so the structural contrast emerges, then a comparison table which is the fastest way to earn the 'main differences' marks, then a concrete case for both. Four steps for limb (b): the heads of cover for each with worked incidents attached rather than listed separately, then a boundary step on collision and general average where both are engaged at once, then a closing analysis of the two different kinds of risk each cover manages.
