first-party loss against third-party loss
commercial underwriter for profit against mutual club owned by members
premium against calls; policy on market forms against club rules
limited by the agreed value against effectively unlimited, save capped heads such as oil pollution
purpose - protect the capital asset, against protect solvency

steps.title: (a) Why a shipowner needs both
points: neither covers the other's field, and each exposure alone can destroy the business
without hull, a total loss destroys the asset and the mortgagee's security
mortgagees therefore require hull cover as a condition of lending
without P&I, liabilities are not bounded by the ship's value at all
pollution, passenger and large cargo claims can exceed the vessel's worth many times
and club entry supports the compulsory-insurance certification without which the ship cannot trade

steps.title: (b) Typical risks covered by H&M, and when it responds
points: perils of the seas, fire and explosion, violent theft, jettison, piracy, contact damage
Inchmaree or negligence clause - boilers, shafts, latent defect, crew, pilot and repairer negligence
subject to due diligence by the assured, and to the deductible
total loss actual or constructive, and particular average
the ship's contribution to general average and salvage, and sue and labour
collision liability to the other ship, traditionally three-fourths
incidents - crankshaft failure, grounding damage, engine-room fire, constructive total loss

steps.title: (b) Typical risks covered by P&I, and when it responds
points: crew illness, injury, death, repatriation, wages and substitutes
passengers and other persons; cargo loss, damage and shortage
pollution liability and clean-up - the one major head carrying a specific monetary cap
wreck removal where compulsory; damage to fixed and floating objects
the collision liability the hull policy does not carry, and any excess
fines, quarantine, diversion, stowaways, life salvage, towage liabilities and legal costs
incidents - bunker overflow, injured oiler, condemned reefer cargo, demolished berth crane

steps.title: (b) The boundary - where both are engaged at once
points: a collision produces two different losses from one event
damage to your own ship is hull; liability to the other ship is split
traditionally three-fourths hull and one-fourth club, plus any excess above the hull limit
modern forms may write collision liability at four-fourths by agreement
if oil is spilled, the pollution liability is entirely the club's
in general average the ship's contribution is a hull claim
and in salvage the reward falls on salved property while special compensation falls on the club

steps.title: (b) Their roles in managing liabilities and operational risk
points: H&M manages capital risk - it converts catastrophic asset loss into a predictable premium
it protects the mortgagee's security and keeps an unfundable repair from becoming insolvency
its discipline is the deductible, and the assumption that the ship is in class and properly manned
P&I manages liability risk and is also a service organisation
correspondents in every port, lawyers and surveyors, security to lift an arrest
certification support, and loss-prevention guidance drawn from the whole entered fleet
its discipline is underwriting the member rather than the risk, and the pay-to-be-paid principle
together they cover the two ways a shipping company fails - losing the ship, or owing more than it is worth

quick_revision.recall_15s: The axis. H&M = 'what happened to MY ship?'; P&I = 'what do I OWE someone else?' H&M. Property cover on hull, machinery and equipment; commercial underwriters writing for profit; fixed premium; agreed value; deductible; standard forms - Institute Time Clauses Hulls, International Hull Clauses, Nordic Plan. Covers perils of the seas, fire, explosion, theft, jettison, piracy, contact damage; plus - under the Inchmaree/negligence clause, subject to due diligence - bursting boilers, breakage of shafts, latent defect, negligence of crew, pilots and repairers; total loss and particular average; GA and salvage contribution; sue and labour; and traditionally 3/4 collision liability. P&I. Third-party liability; written by MUTUAL CLUBS owned by the members - insurer and assured are the same people; funded by CALLS (advance, supplementary, overspill), not premium; cover set by club rules with Board discretion; International Group gives retention - pool - market reinsurance - overspill. Covers CREW (injury, illness, death, repatriation, wages), PASSENGERS, CARGO, POLLUTION (the one head with a specific cap), WRECK REMOVAL, FIXED AND FLOATING OBJECTS, the remaining 1/4 collision and excess, plus fines, stowaways, diversion, legal costs. Why both. No hull, no asset and no mortgage security; no club, no compulsory-insurance certification and no trading. Boundary. One collision = own damage (hull) + liability to the other ship (3/4 hull, 1/4 club) + pollution (all club). Roles. Hull manages capital risk via premium and deductible; club manages liability risk and is also a service organisation - correspondents, security to lift arrest, certification, loss prevention - disciplined by pay to be paid.
critical_numbers: NO MONETARY FIGURE IS QUOTED ANYWHERE - International Group limits, retentions, pooling layers and call rates reset annually and cannot be verified
Collision liability traditionally split three-fourths to hull and one-fourth to the club, with any excess above the hull limit also falling on the club
Modern hull forms may write collision liability at four-fourths by agreement
Oil pollution is the one major head of P&I cover carrying a specific monetary cap rather than effectively unlimited cover
Two limbs at 8 and 8 - an even split, so neither may be treated as the minor one
quick_revision.critical_regulation: The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 is the operative Indian statute for a contract of marine insurance - insurable interest, utmost good faith (s.19), disclosure (s.20), warranties, classification of losses and general average loss (s.66). The UK Marine Insurance Act 1906 is its model but is not the law here, and the UK Insurance Act 2015 does not apply. Beyond that statute there is no governing instrument: the covers themselves are contract and market practice, resting on the standard hull forms and on the individual club's rules. The single regulatory contact point is that compulsory insurance certification under the liability conventions is supported by the club.
quick_revision.major_trap: Citing the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906 in an Indian examination - the operative statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. Then: saying P&I covers damage to the ship, or that H&M covers pollution, either of which destroys the distinction the question is built on; calling a P&I contribution a premium when it is a call; answering limb (b) with more definitions and no incidents when the stem prints the word 'examples'; and quoting monetary limits, which are reset at every renewal.

questions.memory_cue: Two limbs, eight steps, one axis. Limb (a) - define hull (1), define club (2), tabulate the differences (3), say why both are indispensable (4). Limb (b) - hull risks with incidents (5), club risks with incidents (6), the collision and general-average boundary (7), and the two kinds of risk management (8). Walk the club's heads of cover from the inside out: crew, passengers, cargo, pollution, wreck, fixed objects, collision excess, fines and costs.
questions.understand_first: There are exactly two ways a shipping company is destroyed by a single event. It can lose its ship, or it can owe more money than it is worth. Those are completely different problems, and the market solved them in completely different ways - which is the whole content of this question. Losing the ship is an insurable thing: a vessel has a value, that value can be agreed in advance, and a commercial underwriter can price the chance of losing it and make a profit. So hull and machinery cover looks like any other property insurance - a premium, an agreed value, a deductible, standard clauses. Owing money to other people is not like that at all. You cannot value in advance what a pollution incident, a passenger casualty or a lost cargo will cost, and a liability that might be enormous cannot be sensibly written for a fixed premium by someone trying to make a margin on it. So shipowners did the only thing that works: they insured each other. A P&I club is not an insurance company - it is the members, pooling their liabilities, paying calls instead of premiums, writing their own rules, and grouping together internationally so that even a catastrophic claim can be carried. Once you see that the structure follows from the nature of the risk, every difference in the comparison stops being a list to memorise: mutual because unlimited, calls because unpredictable, rules because self-made, and a service organisation because the members want their own problems solved rather than merely paid for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define hull and machinery insurance and P&I insurance in one sentence each.
retrieval_cards.answer: Hull and machinery insurance is a property cover placed in the commercial market which indemnifies the owner for physical loss of or damage to the ship, her machinery and equipment, on an agreed value and subject to a deductible. P&I insurance is a third-party liability cover, written by a mutual association owned by its shipowner members and funded by calls, which indemnifies the owner against his legal liabilities, costs and expenses to others arising out of the operation of the ship.
retrieval_cards.why: The definitions must carry the structural contrast - commercial and property against mutual and liability - because everything else follows from it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which statute governs a contract of marine insurance in an Indian examination?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Marine Insurance Act, 1963. It is modelled on the United Kingdom Marine Insurance Act 1906, but the 1906 Act is not operative here. It supplies insurable interest, the duty of utmost good faith at section 19 and the consequent duty of disclosure at section 20, warranties, the classification of losses, and general average loss at section 66. The UK Insurance Act 2015 reform of the avoidance remedy forms no part of Indian law.
retrieval_cards.why: Citing the 1906 Act is the standing error on Indian marine insurance questions, and much secondary material invites it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is P&I mutual when hull insurance is commercial?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because a ship has a value and a liability does not. A vessel can be valued in advance, so the risk of losing it can be priced and profitably underwritten at a fixed premium. Third-party liabilities cannot be quantified in advance and can exceed the ship's value many times over, so no commercial insurer would write them on effectively unlimited terms for a margin. Shipowners therefore insure each other, contributing by calls, writing their own rules, and grouping internationally so that a catastrophic claim can be shared.
retrieval_cards.why: The structural insight the question is really testing, and it explains every row of the comparison.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the principal heads of P&I cover.
retrieval_cards.answer: Crew illness, injury, death, repatriation and wages; passengers and other persons; cargo loss, damage and shortage; pollution liability and clean-up; wreck removal where compulsory; damage to fixed and floating objects; the portion of collision liability not carried by the hull policy and any excess; and fines, quarantine and diversion expenses, stowaways, life salvage, towage and contractual liabilities and legal costs.
retrieval_cards.why: Eight countable heads. Walking them from the inside out - people, then cargo, then what you damage outside the ship - keeps the list complete under pressure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship collides with another and spills oil. Which insurer pays what?
retrieval_cards.answer: Damage to your own ship is a hull claim. Liability to the other ship and her cargo is split: traditionally three-fourths falls on the hull policy under the running-down clause and the remaining fourth on the club, together with any excess above the hull limit - though modern hull forms may write collision liability at four-fourths by agreement. The pollution liability and clean-up costs are entirely the club's. So one casualty engages the hull underwriter twice and the club twice.
retrieval_cards.why: The single question that tests the whole answer, and the examiner's favourite.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the Inchmaree clause and what does it require of the assured?
retrieval_cards.answer: The negligence clause in the hull policy, which extends cover beyond the traditional perils of the seas to bursting of boilers, breakage of shafts, latent defect in the hull or machinery, and the negligence of the master, officers, crew, pilots, repairers and charterers. It is subject to the assured, owners or managers exercising due diligence, so cover is lost where the loss results from want of diligence at management level.
retrieval_cards.why: The commonest oral follow-up on the hull half, and the due-diligence proviso is the part candidates omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is a P&I club funded, and what is the International Group for?
retrieval_cards.answer: Members pay an advance call at the start of the policy year, a supplementary call if that year's claims exceed expectation, and in an extreme year an overspill call. The International Group lets the mutual system carry catastrophic exposure: each club retains claims up to its own retention, claims above that are pooled and shared among the Group clubs, above the pool sits a collective market reinsurance programme, and above that an overspill arrangement.
retrieval_cards.why: The structure is the mark. No figure should be quoted - retentions and layers are reset at every renewal.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can a ship not trade without P&I entry?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the compulsory insurance certification required under the liability conventions is supported by the club, so a ship not entered with an acceptable club cannot obtain the certificates it needs and will be refused entry to port. In practice club entry is a condition of trading, just as hull cover is a condition of financing - the mortgagee requires it as security for the loan.
retrieval_cards.why: Answers 'why are both essential' concretely rather than as a truism, which is what limb (a) is asking for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Beyond paying claims, what does a P&I club do that a hull underwriter does not?
retrieval_cards.answer: It acts as a service organisation for its members: it maintains correspondents in ports worldwide, instructs lawyers and surveyors, provides security to lift an arrest, supports the compulsory-insurance certification the ship needs to trade, and issues loss-prevention guidance drawn from the claims experience of the whole entered fleet. It also underwrites the member rather than the risk, so a poorly managed owner meets rising calls or is refused entry.
retrieval_cards.why: Half of why P&I matters, and the part candidates leave out when they treat a club as merely another insurer.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the operative statute for a contract of marine insurance in this jurisdiction is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, and the section identities given for utmost good faith, disclosure and general average loss.
reverify_before_publication.why: MIW HOLDS NO COPY OF THE ACT. It is cited by identity and section only and nothing is quoted. The section identities are carried from the repository's own known-traps register (entry 8), which records this as a standing requirement for Indian marine insurance answers precisely because candidates and secondary material routinely cite the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906 instead. Acquiring the 1963 Act would promote this to primary. Note the express caution that the UK Insurance Act 2015 reform of the avoidance remedy forms no part of Indian law.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Every statement in this answer about what hull and machinery cover and P&I cover actually cover, including the heads of cover, the Inchmaree clause extensions, the mutual structure, the call system and the International Group architecture.
reverify_before_publication.why: MIW HOLDS NO POLICY WORDING, NO INSTITUTE OR INTERNATIONAL HULL CLAUSES, NO CLUB RULE BOOK AND NO POOLING AGREEMENT, and these are commercial documents rather than public instruments, so this is not a gap ordinary corpus acquisition closes. Everything is authoritative restatement or industry practice, classified P2 or P3; no clause is quoted and no clause number is asserted. It ships as-is because the propositions are settled market understanding and the limitation is stated in the answer itself.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no monetary figure of any kind appears anywhere in this answer - no oil-pollution limit, passenger or crew limit, club retention, pooling layer, reinsurance or overspill figure, premium, call rate, deductible or claims statistic.
reverify_before_publication.why: THE ONLY GENUINE CURRENCY EXPOSURE ON THIS QUESTION, AND IT IS CLOSED BY OMISSION RATHER THAN BY A GUESS. International Group limits and layers are reset annually at renewal and MIW holds no source for them, so any figure given as at November 2024 would be unverifiable. A later session must not read this as a gap and fill it with the figure current at the time of reading, which would silently mis-date the answer.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That collision liability is traditionally carried three-fourths by the hull policy under the running-down clause, with the remaining fourth and any excess falling on the club.
reverify_before_publication.why: This is the settled market convention and is what the examiner expects, but it is not invariable - modern hull forms may write collision liability at four-fourths by agreement, and which applies depends on the actual policy. The answer states the variation rather than flattening a conditional statement into a categorical one. Recorded so that no derived layer - flashcard, recall line or cheat sheet - reduces it to an unqualified rule.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no clause-set edition year is given for the Institute Time Clauses, the International Hull Clauses or the Nordic Marine Insurance Plan.
reverify_before_publication.why: Each has been revised more than once and MIW holds none of them, so an edition stated as current at November 2024 could not be verified. The forms are named by identity only, which is all the question requires. A deliberate omission, recorded so it is not later read as a gap.

blocks.h: 1. What the operative Strategy is, and what it replaced

blocks.p: The governing instrument is the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, adopted by resolution MEPC.377(80) on 7 July 2023. It expressly revokes the 2018 Initial Strategy from that date, so the Initial Strategy's targets are no longer the answer to this question. It is a policy instrument, not law: it binds nobody directly and works by committing the Committee to develop measures which then become law as amendments to MARPOL Annex VI. It is to be kept under review with a view to a further revised Strategy in 2028.

blocks.h: 2. The vision, the levels of ambition and the indicative checkpoints

blocks.p: The vision is to reduce GHG emissions from international shipping and, as a matter of urgency, to phase them out as soon as possible, while promoting a just and equitable transition. Four levels of ambition follow: the carbon intensity of the ship to decline through better design of new ships; the carbon intensity of international shipping to decline, with CO2 per transport work down at least 40% by 2030 against 2008; the uptake of zero or near-zero GHG technologies, fuels and energy sources to reach at least 5%, striving for 10%, of the energy used by 2030; and to peak emissions as soon as possible and reach net-zero GHG emissions by or around, i.e. close to, 2050.

The indicative checkpoints are different in kind and this is where marks are lost. They are absolute, not intensity-based - to reduce total annual GHG emissions, against 2008, by at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030, and by at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040. So 40% is intensity and 20% is absolute, both by 2030 and both against 2008. Two further features matter: the targets are GHG, not CO2 alone, so methane counts; and they are measured well-to-wake under the LCA guidelines, MEPC.376(80).

blocks.h: 3. The pathway - short, mid and long term as the Strategy defines them

blocks.p: The Strategy defines the three horizons by timing, not by subject matter:

ul: Short-term measures - those finalized and agreed between 2018 and 2023. These are already law in MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 and are the subject of the second half of this question.

Mid-term measures - a basket to be finalized and agreed by the Committee by 2025, comprising both a technical element - a goal-based marine fuel standard regulating the phased reduction of the GHG intensity of marine fuel - and an economic element, on the basis of a maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism. The Strategy requires both together, and requires synergies with existing measures such as the carbon intensity indicator to be considered.

Long-term measures - deliberately undefined. They are described only as measures finalized and agreed beyond 2030, to be developed as part of the 2028 review. There is no list, and inventing one would be fabrication.

blocks.h: 4. Where the process stood at this examination

blocks.p: The Strategy's own milestone table places this sitting. MEPC 81 (spring 2024) has happened, and so has MEPC 82, which sat from 30 September to 4 October 2024 - the session at which the finalized comprehensive impact assessment was due. What has not happened is anything binding: approval of the measures is scheduled for MEPC 83 in spring 2025, adoption at an extraordinary MEPC session about six months later, and entry into force 16 months after adoption. So the position at this date is stated in one sentence: the architecture of the mid-term basket is agreed and nothing in it is adopted. Any answer describing a binding IMO carbon price or fuel-intensity limit as existing law is wrong for November 2024.
The two short-term measures were adopted together by resolution MEPC.328(76) on 17 June 2021, entered into force on 1 November 2022 and applied from 1 January 2023. The first is technical.

The Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index extends to the existing fleet the design discipline the EEDI had imposed only on newbuildings. Each existing ship above the applicable size threshold must calculate an attained EEXI - regulation 23 - representing the CO2 emitted per tonne-mile of transport capacity from its design characteristics, and that attained value must be no greater than the required EEXI for its type and size - regulation 25. It is a one-off, design-based requirement, verified at the first annual, intermediate or renewal survey on or after 1 January 2023 and endorsed on the ship's International Energy Efficiency Certificate.

Because the index is calculated from design parameters, most existing ships comply not by rebuilding but by limiting installed power - a shaft power limitation or engine power limitation, with the limitation recorded in an onboard management manual and an emergency override available to the master when full power is needed for safety. A minority achieve compliance by energy saving devices, hull and propeller improvements or derating.

blocks.h: 6. The second short-term measure - the operational carbon intensity rating

blocks.p: The second is operational, and it is the one that bites every year. Under regulation 28, a ship above the applicable size threshold must determine its attained annual operational carbon intensity indicator from the fuel oil consumption data it already reports under the data collection system at regulation 27, and compare it with the required annual operational CII.

The ship is then given a rating from A to E - A being the best. The consequences are graduated rather than penal: a ship rated D for three consecutive years, or E for a single year, must develop a plan of corrective actions in Part III of its SEEMP, and that plan must be approved. The SEEMP itself is required by regulation 26, and compliance is evidenced by a Statement of Compliance. The rating is therefore a continuous operational obligation where the EEXI is a one-off design check - which is the essential contrast between the two.

blocks.h: 7. The guidelines that make the two measures workable

blocks.p: Neither measure could operate on the regulation text alone, because both depend on calculation methods and reference values that had to be agreed separately. That is what the question means by with their guidelines.
For the carbon intensity indicator there are five, lettered G1 to G5:

ol: G1 - MEPC.352(78), adopted 10 June 2022: the operational carbon intensity indicators and the calculation methods.
G2 - MEPC.353(78), 10 June 2022: the reference lines against which a ship's performance is judged.
G3 - MEPC.338(76), adopted 17 June 2021: the reduction factors applied to those reference lines year by year, which is what makes the requirement tighten over time.
G4 - MEPC.354(78), 10 June 2022: the rating of ships, that is the A to E boundaries.

G5 - MEPC.355(78), 10 June 2022: interim guidelines on correction factors and voyage adjustments, which prevent a ship being penalised for time spent in ice, at anchor awaiting berth, or on other voyages outside its ordinary trade.

blocks.p: Sitting alongside them are the SEEMP development guidelines, and the edition matters at this date. The operative guidelines are the 2024 Guidelines for the development of a SEEMP, resolution MEPC.395(82), adopted 4 October 2024 - one month before this examination - whose operative paragraph 3 revokes the 2022 Guidelines, MEPC.346(78). They set out the SEEMP in three parts: Part I, the ship management plan to improve energy efficiency; Part II, the fuel oil consumption data-collection plan; and Part III, the ship operational carbon intensity plan in which the required CII for the next three years, the implementation plan and any corrective actions are recorded.

For the EEXI there is a corresponding set covering the method of calculating the attained EEXI, the survey and certification procedure, and the shaft and engine power limitation route to compliance including the management manual and override arrangements.

blocks.h: 8. What the two measures do in practice, and the limits of the short-term approach

blocks.p: Together they attack the problem from both ends: EEXI constrains what the ship is, and CII constrains how she is used. In practice the effects are commercial as much as technical. Power limitation caps the speed that can be offered, which changes what the ship can be chartered for. An annual rating is a public performance grade, so charterers began to ask for it and lenders to price it, and clauses allocating responsibility for the rating between owner and charterer became necessary - because the party that decides the speed and the party that holds the certificate are usually not the same.

The limits are equally clear, and stating them answers the word discuss. Both measures are tank-to-wake in effect - they reward burning less fuel, not burning better fuel - so neither creates any real incentive to adopt a zero-carbon fuel. Both are intensity measures, so a growing fleet can improve its rating while total emissions rise, which is precisely why the Strategy also carries absolute checkpoints. And the CII is acknowledged to reward slow steaming and long ballast legs in ways that do not always reflect real efficiency. That is the reason the mid-term basket exists at all: a well-to-wake goal-based fuel standard plus a price on emissions is designed to reach exactly what the short-term measures cannot.

The stem sets two distinct tasks and the second is far more specific than candidates expect. First, briefly discuss the ambitions and pathways with focus on short, mid and long-term goals. Second - and note the change of command verb - explain the two short-term measures approved by the IMO for implementation, with their guidelines.

The word briefly governs the first half and is an instruction, not a courtesy: the examiner is telling you not to spend the paper on the Strategy. The word guidelines governs the second half and is where the discriminating marks are. Almost every candidate can describe EEXI and CII; very few can name the guideline layer that makes them operable. Steps 5 to 7 are therefore where this answer earns its marks, and step 7 is the single highest-value paragraph on the question.

EEXI and the operational carbon intensity rating (CII). Both were adopted together by MEPC.328(76) on 17 June 2021, entered into force 1 November 2022 and applied from 1 January 2023. One is technical and one-off; the other is operational and annual. If you hold only that contrast you can construct both descriptions.

Do not answer 'EEDI and SEEMP'. The EEDI applies to newbuildings and long predates the short-term measure package; the SEEMP is the vehicle through which the CII obligation is discharged, not a separate measure. Saying so explicitly is a good discriminator.

blocks.h: The MARPOL Annex VI numbers, and the trap in them

blocks.p: The 2021 revised Annex VI entered into force on 1 November 2022 and renumbered chapter 4. Most published material still carries the old scheme, so a well-read candidate is the one most likely to get this wrong.

ul: Regulation 21 - Functional requirements. It is not EEDI. This is the trap.
22 - attained EEDI; 24 - required EEDI.
23 - attained EEXI; 25 - required EEXI.
26 - SEEMP; 27 - fuel oil consumption data collection; 28 - operational carbon intensity.

blocks.p: If the numbers desert you under pressure, name the measures and do not guess. A correct measure with no number scores; a confident wrong number invites a probe.

blocks.h: Get the two families of Strategy numbers apart

ul: Levels of ambition are mostly intensity: CO2 per transport work down at least 40% by 2030; zero or near-zero fuels at at least 5%, striving for 10%, of energy used by 2030; and net zero by or around 2050.
Indicative checkpoints are absolute: total annual GHG emissions down at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030 and at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040.

blocks.p: So 40 is intensity, 20 is absolute, both by 2030 and both against 2008. Write them under separate headings and the confusion cannot happen. Never drop the 'striving for' figures - they are half of each checkpoint.

blocks.h: The date of this paper - the sharpest edge on the question

blocks.p: MEPC 82 sat from 30 September to 4 October 2024, before this examination. That single fact separates a November 2024 answer from a September 2024 one, and it has one concrete consequence you must get right:

ul: The operative SEEMP guidelines are the 2024 Guidelines, MEPC.395(82), adopted 4 October 2024, which revoked MEPC.346(78). A September 2024 answer citing MEPC.346(78) would be correct; the same answer in November is wrong.
The chain is worth holding whole: MEPC.346(78) of 2022, amended by MEPC.388(81) at MEPC 81 in March 2024, then revoked and replaced by MEPC.395(82) in October 2024.

blocks.p: In the other direction, the IMO Net-Zero Framework and the GHG Fuel Intensity measure did not exist at this sitting - they came out of MEPC 83 in April 2025. Writing them in is the single most likely way to be wrong on this question today, because almost all current material on IMO decarbonisation uses that vocabulary.

ul: Answering EEDI and SEEMP as the two short-term measures. It is EEXI and CII.
Citing MEPC.346(78) as the current SEEMP guidelines. It was revoked on 4 October 2024, one month before this paper.
Naming the Net-Zero Framework or GFI. They did not exist - MEPC 83, April 2025.
Quoting the 2018 Initial Strategy targets. The 2023 Strategy revoked it.
Saying 'net zero by 2050' flatly. The text is 'by or around, i.e. close to, 2050'.
Confusing the two families of numbers - 40% intensity, 20% absolute.
Describing the mid-term measures as one measure. It is a basket of two, technical and economic, required together.
Inventing long-term measures. The Strategy defines them only by timing.
Answering 'with their guidelines' by naming none. That is where the marks are.
Quoting a CII reduction factor or rating boundary. Those come from the guidelines for a specific ship type, size and year.
Using regulation 21 for EEDI - that is the pre-2021 numbering.
Name the two short-term measures. EEXI and the operational carbon intensity rating.
Which is technical and which operational? EEXI is technical and one-off; CII is operational and annual.
How does a ship usually achieve EEXI compliance? By shaft or engine power limitation, with a management manual and an emergency override.
What happens to a ship rated D three years running? A plan of corrective actions in SEEMP Part III, which must be approved.
Name the CII guidelines. G1 calculation, G2 reference lines, G3 reduction factors, G4 rating, G5 correction factors and voyage adjustments.
Which SEEMP guidelines apply at this date? The 2024 Guidelines, MEPC.395(82), which revoked MEPC.346(78) in October 2024.
What is in SEEMP Part III? The ship operational carbon intensity plan - required CII for the next three years, the implementation plan, self-evaluation and any corrective actions.
Is the mid-term basket law yet? No. Approval was scheduled for MEPC 83 in spring 2025 and adoption for an extraordinary session thereafter.
Why is a mid-term basket needed at all if EEXI and CII exist? Because both short-term measures reward burning less fuel rather than better fuel, and both are intensity-based.
What replaced the 2018 Initial Strategy, and when?
State the 2030 and 2040 indicative checkpoints with the striving figures.
Is that 40% absolute or intensity?
What are the two elements of the mid-term basket?
Which regulation carries attained EEXI? And SEEMP?
Explain shaft power limitation and the override.
How is the attained CII calculated, and from what data?
What are the rating bands and what triggers corrective action?
Which resolution carries the current SEEMP guidelines, and what did it revoke?

blocks.p: Eight steps in two blocks matching the two printed demands. THE STRATEGY (briefly) - the instrument and what it revoked (1), ambitions and checkpoints (2), the three horizons (3), where we actually stand (4). THE TWO MEASURES (in detail) - EEXI (5), CII (6), THE GUIDELINES (7), and what they do and cannot do (8).
For the measures: EEXI is what the ship IS; CII is what the ship DOES. One-off against annual; design against operation; certificate endorsement against an A-to-E grade.

For the five CII guidelines walk the calculation in order: how you work it out (G1), what you compare it against (G2), how much tighter each year (G3), what grade that earns (G4), and what does not count against you (G5). Then SEEMP Part III is where the answer is written down.
For the Strategy numbers hold one pair and one hedge: 40 intensity and 20 absolute by 2030, 70 by 2040, and net zero by or around 2050. Every 'at least' has a 'striving for' behind it.

blocks.p: The evidence position on this answer is strong and almost entirely primary. MEPC.377(80), MEPC.328(76), MEPC.395(82) and all five CII guidelines were read at source from copies held in the MIW True Source corpus, and every target, date, regulation number and resolution identity above was read off the instrument rather than recalled.

Three limits are declared. The EEXI guideline resolutions are not held, so that part of step 7 describes them by function and no resolution number has been invented for them - a deliberate refusal to guess. MEPC.376(80) was not read; it is named only because MEPC.377(80) points to it, and only the well-to-wake principle stated in MEPC.377(80) itself is used. And no CII reduction factor, rating boundary, reference-line value or required-EEXI reduction percentage is quoted anywhere, because those are read from the guidelines for a particular ship type, size band and calendar year, and a general figure would be false precision.

One further honesty. The specific business outcome of MEPC 82 on the mid-term measures is not asserted. What is stated is what the Strategy's own milestone table schedules for that session, and - decisively - that nothing in the basket was adopted at this sitting, which follows from the milestone table itself since adoption is scheduled for an extraordinary session after MEPC 83.

Finally the currency warning, which matters more here than anywhere else on the paper. This answer is anchored to November 2024 and must not be updated in place. The measures were approved, renamed and reshaped from April 2025 onwards, and the correct answer for a later paper is a different answer. What makes this one right is precisely that it stops where the Organization had actually got to - after MEPC 82, before MEPC 83.

notes: THIS IS THE HIGHEST-RISK QUESTION ON THE PAPER, ALONGSIDE Q2, AND THE RISK IS ANACHRONISM IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. Almost every piece of study material now written on IMO decarbonisation uses vocabulary that did not exist in November 2024; and the September 2024 treatment in the corpus is already stale in the other direction.

THE DEFINING FACT: MEPC 82 SAT 30 SEPTEMBER TO 4 OCTOBER 2024, BEFORE THIS SITTING. This inverts three findings carried in the committed September 2024 anchor and is what makes a November answer different from a September one.

SUPERSEDED BEFORE THIS SITTING: MEPC.346(78), the 2022 SEEMP Guidelines, was REVOKED by MEPC.395(82) on 4 OCTOBER 2024 - one month before this examination. The chain is MEPC.346(78), amended by MEPC.388(81) at MEPC 81 in March 2024, then revoked and replaced by MEPC.395(82). A September 2024 answer citing MEPC.346(78) is correct; the same citation here is WRONG. Established by reading MEPC.395(82) operative paragraph 3 at source.
OPERATIVE: MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023, read in full at source. It revoked the 2018 Initial Strategy from that date, so the Initial Strategy targets must not be given.

OPERATIVE: the two short-term measures, adopted by MEPC.328(76) on 17 June 2021, in force 1 November 2022, applying from 1 January 2023. At this sitting 2023 is a complete data year and ratings have been issued against it.
OPERATIVE: the CII guideline set G1 to G5 - MEPC.352(78), MEPC.353(78), MEPC.338(76), MEPC.354(78), MEPC.355(78) - all read at source and all adopted well before the sitting.

NOT YET AVAILABLE - MUST APPEAR NOWHERE: the IMO NET-ZERO FRAMEWORK and the GHG FUEL INTENSITY (GFI) measure, and any draft MARPOL Annex VI chapter carrying them. Those arose at MEPC 83 in April 2025, five months after this sitting. Neither term is used anywhere in this answer. These are the single most dangerous contamination sources on the paper and the reason QP2508-Q8 and QP2602-Q8 were refused absolutely as donors.

NOTHING IN THE MID-TERM BASKET IS ADOPTED. Per MEPC.377(80) section 6.2, approval was scheduled for MEPC 83 in spring 2025, adoption for an extraordinary session about six months later, and entry into force 16 months after adoption. The answer states this expressly at step 4.
THE PRECISE MEPC 82 BUSINESS OUTCOME IS NOT ASSERTED, only that the session had taken place and that nothing was adopted - which follows from the milestone table itself.

ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE, AND CORRECTLY ABSENT: MEPC.385(81), adopted 22 March 2024, enters into force 1 August 2025; MEPC.392(82), adopted 4 October 2024, enters into force 1 March 2026. Neither is a short-term GHG measure and neither is cited as operative.

NO DONOR WAS ACCEPTED, SO THERE IS NO DONOR CONTAMINATION ROUTE. QP2409-Q3 was rejected partly BECAUSE it is pre-MEPC 82. QP2412-Q8 (December 2024) independently corroborates the MEPC.395(82) position and was used only as corroboration.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two printed demands with different command verbs and different depths. First, BRIEFLY DISCUSS the IMO decarbonisation ambitions and pathways with focus on the short-term, mid-term and long-term goals - the word 'briefly' is an instruction limiting this half. Second, EXPLAIN THE TWO SHORT-TERM MEASURES APPROVED BY THE IMO FOR IMPLEMENTATION, WITH THEIR GUIDELINES. The second demand is far more specific than it looks: it requires the candidate to identify exactly two measures, to explain each, and to name the guideline layer beneath them. That guideline requirement is what separates this question from every other decarbonisation question in the corpus.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 printed against the whole question with no sub-division. The word 'briefly' governs the first half, so roughly six marks for the Strategy - instrument, ambitions, checkpoints and the three horizons - and roughly ten for the two short-term measures and their guidelines. Within that second block, roughly three marks for EEXI, three for the operational carbon intensity rating, three for the guidelines, and one to two for the practical and critical closing. The sitting-position step is paid for out of the first block because it is what makes the pathway answer correct for November 2024.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate identifies the two short-term measures correctly as EEXI and the operational carbon intensity rating - not EEDI and SEEMP - can state which is technical and which operational, knows how EEXI compliance is achieved in practice, knows the rating bands and what triggers corrective action, CAN NAME THE GUIDELINES rather than merely alluding to them, and can state the Strategy's ambitions and checkpoints without confusing intensity with absolute reduction. At management level the examiner also expects the candidate to know that the mid-term basket was not yet law.

All five CII guidelines read at source for identity and adoption date, since the stem expressly asks for the guidelines

decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: HIGH - and uniquely in BOTH directions. Forwards: the mid-term measures were approved, renamed and reshaped from MEPC 83 in April 2025, and nearly all current material uses vocabulary - Net-Zero Framework, GHG Fuel Intensity - that did not exist at this sitting. Backwards: the September 2024 answer already in the corpus states that MEPC 82 has not happened and that MEPC.395(82) does not exist, and both statements are false here. This question sits in a five-week window between two guideline editions and must be written for it precisely.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW - the Strategy and the measures are IMO instruments applying through MARPOL Annex VI. No regional measure is relied on and no Indian implementing provision is asserted. The EU measures are not needed for this question and are not introduced.
technical_ambiguities: 'The two short-term measures' is the crux and is genuinely capable of being misread. The Strategy defines short-term measures by TIMING - those finalized and agreed between 2018 and 2023 - which is a wider class. But the two measures 'approved for implementation' with a guideline layer of their own are EEXI and the operational carbon intensity rating, adopted together by MEPC.328(76). The answer identifies them expressly and says why EEDI and SEEMP are not the answer.

'With their guidelines' could be answered with a single sentence. It is the highest-value part of the question and is given its own step, naming the five CII guidelines by letter and resolution and the SEEMP guidelines by edition.

'Long-term goals' invites a list of long-term measures. There is none: the Strategy defines them only by timing, beyond 2030 and to be developed in the 2028 review. Inventing a list would be fabrication and the answer says so.

'Ambitions' is loose. The Strategy distinguishes LEVELS OF AMBITION from INDICATIVE CHECKPOINTS, and the two use different measures - intensity per transport work against total annual emissions. The answer separates them.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Four compact steps for the Strategy half, held short by the word 'briefly' - the instrument and what it revoked, the two families of numbers, the three horizons defined by timing, and a step fixing where the process actually stood at this sitting. Then four fuller steps for the second demand - EEXI, the carbon intensity rating, a dedicated step on the guidelines because that is the printed requirement most candidates miss, and a closing step on what the measures do in practice and where they reach their limit, which answers the command verb 'discuss' in the first half.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: Two instruments carry this answer. Resolution MEPC.377(80), the 2023 Strategy, which by operative paragraph 6 revokes the 2018 Initial Strategy and by section 4.5 requires the mid-term basket to contain both a goal-based marine fuel standard and a GHG pricing mechanism. And resolution MEPC.328(76), the 2021 Revised MARPOL Annex VI, in force 1 November 2022, which introduced the two short-term measures - attained EEXI at regulation 23 against required EEXI at regulation 25, and operational carbon intensity at regulation 28 fed by the data collection system at regulation 27 and discharged through the SEEMP at regulation 26.
quick_revision.major_trap: Three traps, and the middle one is specific to this sitting. First, naming the wrong two measures: it is EEXI and the operational carbon intensity rating, not EEDI and SEEMP - EEDI applies to newbuildings and the SEEMP is the vehicle, not a separate measure. Second, citing MEPC.346(78) as the current SEEMP guidelines: it was revoked by MEPC.395(82) on 4 October 2024, one month before this examination, so a September 2024 answer is correct and the same words here are wrong. Third, writing a post-2025 answer into a 2024 paper: the IMO Net-Zero Framework and the GHG Fuel Intensity measure came out of MEPC 83 in April 2025 and did not exist at this sitting.

questions.memory_cue: Eight steps in the two blocks the stem prints. THE STRATEGY, briefly - instrument and revocation (1), the two families of numbers (2), the three horizons defined by timing (3), where we actually stand (4). THE TWO MEASURES, in detail - EEXI, what the ship IS (5), the rating, what the ship DOES (6), THE GUIDELINES (7), and what they cannot reach (8). For the five CII guidelines walk the calculation: how you work it out, what you compare against, how much tighter each year, what grade that earns, what does not count against you.
questions.understand_first: Read this question as two layers that were built ten years apart and are trying to solve the same problem at different speeds. The Strategy is the Organization writing down, in one place, how much shipping must reduce, by when, and by what process the binding rules will be produced. It is not law and it makes nobody do anything; it is a schedule for making law, and it deliberately splits that schedule into three horizons defined purely by timing - what was agreed by 2023, what must be agreed by 2025, and what will not even be designed until the 2028 review. The short-term measures are the part of that schedule which has already been delivered, and they are the only part that is actually binding on your ship. There are two of them and they attack the problem from opposite ends. EEXI asks what the ship is: a one-off calculation from her design, done once, satisfied for most ships by simply capping the power she is allowed to use. The carbon intensity rating asks what the ship does: an annual measurement from the fuel she actually burned, producing a public grade from A to E that follows her around the market. One is a certificate; the other is a report card that arrives every year. And the reason a mid-term basket exists at all is that both of these measures only reward burning less fuel - neither of them cares what the fuel is made of. That is the gap a goal-based fuel standard and a carbon price are meant to close. Finally, note where this paper sits: MEPC 82 finished four weeks before the examination, so the SEEMP guidelines had just been replaced, and the mid-term measures were fully designed and not yet adopted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the IMO decarbonisation and short-term measures question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The Strategy and what it revoked. 2 Ambitions and indicative checkpoints. 3 The three horizons defined by timing. 4 Where the process stood at this sitting. 5 EEXI. 6 The operational carbon intensity rating. 7 The guidelines. 8 What the measures do and cannot do.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem prints 'briefly' for the Strategy half and 'explain ... with their guidelines' for the second, so the weight belongs in steps 5 to 7.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the two short-term measures approved by the IMO for implementation.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index, EEXI, which is technical and one-off, and the operational carbon intensity indicator rating, which is operational and annual. Both were adopted together by resolution MEPC.328(76) on 17 June 2021, entered into force on 1 November 2022 and applied from 1 January 2023. They are not EEDI and SEEMP: the EEDI applies to newbuildings and long predates the package, and the SEEMP is the vehicle through which the CII obligation is discharged rather than a separate measure.
retrieval_cards.why: Identifying the wrong two measures loses the larger half of the question at the first sentence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the levels of ambition and the indicative checkpoints, and say how they differ.
retrieval_cards.answer: Levels of ambition: carbon intensity of new ships to improve by design; CO2 per transport work down by at least 40% by 2030 against 2008; zero or near-zero technologies, fuels and energy sources to be at least 5%, striving for 10%, of the energy used by 2030; and net-zero GHG emissions by or around, i.e. close to, 2050. Indicative checkpoints: total annual GHG emissions down at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030 and at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040, both against 2008. They differ because the checkpoints are measured on total absolute emissions whereas the corresponding ambition is measured on intensity.
retrieval_cards.why: 40% intensity against 20% absolute, both by 2030 against 2008, is the most confused pair of numbers on this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain the EEXI requirement and how ships comply in practice.
retrieval_cards.answer: Each existing ship above the applicable size threshold must calculate an attained EEXI under regulation 23, representing CO2 emitted per tonne-mile of transport capacity derived from her design characteristics, and that value must not exceed the required EEXI for her type and size under regulation 25. It is a one-off design-based check verified at the first annual, intermediate or renewal survey on or after 1 January 2023 and endorsed on the International Energy Efficiency Certificate. Because it is calculated from design parameters, most ships comply by shaft or engine power limitation, recorded in an onboard management manual with an emergency override available to the master, rather than by physical modification.
retrieval_cards.why: The power-limitation route is what makes EEXI a practical rather than a theoretical measure, and the override is the detail examiners probe.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain the operational carbon intensity rating and its consequences.
retrieval_cards.answer: Under regulation 28 a ship above the applicable threshold determines her attained annual operational CII from the fuel oil consumption data reported under the data collection system at regulation 27, and compares it with the required annual operational CII. She is then rated from A to E. A ship rated D for three consecutive years, or E for a single year, must develop a plan of corrective actions in Part III of her SEEMP, required by regulation 26, and that plan must be approved. Compliance is evidenced by a Statement of Compliance.
retrieval_cards.why: The rating trigger - D for three years or E for one - is the most commonly misremembered detail in the measure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the CII guidelines G1 to G5 and say what each does.
retrieval_cards.answer: G1, resolution MEPC.352(78), the operational carbon intensity indicators and calculation methods. G2, MEPC.353(78), the reference lines. G3, MEPC.338(76), the reduction factors applied to those reference lines year by year. G4, MEPC.354(78), the rating of ships, that is the A to E boundaries. G5, MEPC.355(78), interim guidelines on correction factors and voyage adjustments.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for the measures 'with their guidelines'. Naming all five is the single highest-value thing on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which SEEMP guidelines were operative at this sitting, and why does the date matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2024 Guidelines for the development of a SEEMP, resolution MEPC.395(82), adopted on 4 October 2024, whose operative paragraph 3 revokes the 2022 Guidelines, MEPC.346(78). The date matters because MEPC 82 sat from 30 September to 4 October 2024, four weeks before this examination, so an answer written for a September 2024 sitting would correctly cite MEPC.346(78) and the same citation here would be wrong. The full chain is MEPC.346(78) of 2022, amended by MEPC.388(81) at MEPC 81 in March 2024, then revoked and replaced by MEPC.395(82).
retrieval_cards.why: This is the one fact that distinguishes a November 2024 answer from a September 2024 one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where had the mid-term measures actually got to by November 2024?
retrieval_cards.answer: The architecture was agreed and nothing was adopted. Under the Strategy's own milestone table, MEPC 81 in spring 2024 had finalized the basket, MEPC 82 had sat from 30 September to 4 October 2024, approval of the measures was scheduled for MEPC 83 in spring 2025, adoption for an extraordinary session about six months after that, and entry into force 16 months after adoption. The IMO Net-Zero Framework and the GHG Fuel Intensity measure did not exist at this sitting - they came out of MEPC 83 in April 2025.
retrieval_cards.why: Writing a post-2025 answer into a 2024 paper is the commonest way to get this question wrong today.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is a mid-term basket needed if EEXI and CII already exist?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because both short-term measures are tank-to-wake in effect and intensity-based. They reward burning less fuel, not burning better fuel, so neither creates any real incentive to adopt a zero or near-zero carbon fuel; and because they measure intensity, a growing fleet can improve its ratings while total emissions still rise. The mid-term basket answers both gaps directly: a goal-based marine fuel standard regulating the well-to-wake GHG intensity of the fuel, and an economic element pricing emissions.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the closing evaluation, and it links the two halves of the question into one argument rather than two lists.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The whole sitting-position analysis at step 4 - that MEPC 82 had taken place before this examination, that the operative SEEMP guidelines were therefore MEPC.395(82) and not MEPC.346(78), and that nothing in the mid-term basket was adopted at November 2024.
reverify_before_publication.why: This is date-driven and it is the load-bearing claim of the answer. It is established from MEPC.395(82) read at source - adopted 4 October 2024, operative paragraph 3 revoking MEPC.346(78) - together with the section 6.2 milestone table of MEPC.377(80), also read at source. THIS ANSWER IS ANCHORED TO NOVEMBER 2024 AND MUST NOT BE UPDATED IN PLACE. The danger runs in BOTH directions here, uniquely on this paper: forwards, a later reader may import the Net-Zero Framework and GFI from MEPC 83 in April 2025; backwards, a reader aligning this answer with the committed September 2024 treatment would re-import MEPC.346(78), which is stale by one month at this sitting.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the EEXI calculation, survey and certification, and shaft or engine power limitation guidelines are described by FUNCTION and that no resolution number is asserted for any of them.
reverify_before_publication.why: MIW DOES NOT HOLD THESE RESOLUTIONS. This is a deliberate refusal to guess on a question that expressly asks for the measures 'with their guidelines', where the temptation to complete the set with an invented number is at its strongest. The five CII guidelines and the SEEMP guidelines WERE read at source and are given in full, so the asymmetry in the answer is real and is visible to the reader. Acquiring the EEXI guideline resolutions would promote that part of step 7 to primary and is recorded as an acquisition need.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the specific business outcome of MEPC 82 on the mid-term measures is not asserted, only that the session had taken place and that nothing was adopted.
reverify_before_publication.why: The Strategy's section 6.2 milestone table schedules the finalized comprehensive impact assessment report for MEPC 82, and that is what the answer says. What the session actually resolved is not stated, because no held source establishes it. The conclusion the answer relies on - that nothing in the basket was adopted at November 2024 - does not depend on the session's business at all: it follows from the milestone table itself, since approval is scheduled for MEPC 83 and adoption for an extraordinary session thereafter.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no CII reduction factor, rating boundary, reference-line value or required-EEXI reduction percentage is quoted anywhere.
reverify_before_publication.why: Those values are read from guidelines G2, G3 and G4 for a particular ship type, size band and calendar year, and from the required-EEXI table for a particular ship type and size. A single figure presented as general would be false precision, and the reduction factors in particular tighten year by year so any figure would also silently date the answer. A deliberate omission, recorded so a later session does not read it as a gap and fill it.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The analysis at step 8 - that both short-term measures are tank-to-wake in effect and intensity-based, that a growing fleet can improve its rating while total emissions rise, and the resulting commercial consequences for chartering and finance.
reverify_before_publication.why: Engineering and commercial judgement reasoned from the measures themselves, not a finding of the Organization, and declared as such. It is nonetheless the part of the answer that connects the two printed demands into a single argument, so it is deliberately reasoned rather than recalled. No cost, freight-rate or compliance-cost figure is quoted anywhere.

blocks.h: 1. (a) Where the 80 per cent claim comes from, and what it is

blocks.p: The figure is quoted everywhere and is almost always misused. It does not come from a study which established that four accidents in five are caused by a defective human being. It is an artefact of how investigations attribute causes. An investigator works backwards from the damage and stops when a satisfying answer appears - and because a person is present at the end of almost every chain of events, the last human act before the loss is nearly always available as an answer.

So the statement is better read as: in about 80 per cent of accidents, a human action or decision can be identified in the causal chain. That is close to a tautology in a system operated by people, and it says almost nothing about what should be done. Two things follow. It is not a finding, it is a stopping rule. And treating it as a finding produces the wrong response - exhortation, blame and another procedure - because if the cause is a careless individual, the cure appears to be a more careful one.

blocks.h: 2. (a) What 'a complex hierarchical socio-technical system' means for a ship

blocks.p: The phrase in the question is the corrective, and each word does work.

ul: Socio-technical - the ship is not a machine with an operator attached. Performance is produced by people and technology together, plus the procedures and the environment. Neither half can be assessed alone.

Complex - the parts are tightly coupled and interact in ways not fully foreseeable. A change made for one good reason - a new alarm, a revised checklist, a reduced crew - has effects elsewhere that nobody designed.

Hierarchical - and this is the decisive word. The system has layers: the regulator and flag State, the classification society, the shipyard and equipment designer, the company and its shore management, the master, and finally the watchkeeper with his hand on the valve. Decisions taken at the upper layers - manning levels, maintenance budget, schedule pressure, equipment selection, procedure design - create the conditions in which the person at the lowest layer acts.

blocks.p: The consequence is the heart of limb (a). Accidents in such a system are not usually caused by one failure. They occur when latent conditions, created earlier and elsewhere by people who were nowhere near the ship at the time, lie dormant until they combine with an active failure at the sharp end and with the particular circumstances of the day. The defences that should have stopped it - design, procedure, training, supervision, alarms - each had a gap, and on that occasion the gaps lined up.

blocks.h: 3. (a) What 'human error' therefore means here, and what follows

blocks.p: Read against that system, 'human error' denotes the last human action in a chain, at the sharp end, where the investigation happened to stop. It is a label applied at the point where somebody ceased to ask 'why'. It is therefore a symptom, not a cause - the visible end of a process whose real determinants lie upstream in design, staffing, scheduling and management decision.

Two management consequences follow, and they are what a management-level candidate is being examined on. First, the correct question after an incident is not 'who erred?' but 'why did this action make sense to a competent person at the time, given what he had in front of him?' - because it almost always did. Second, errors cannot be eliminated by instructing people not to make them. They are reduced by changing the conditions that produce them: better interfaces, workable procedures, adequate manning and rest, honest reporting and a management system that acts on what is reported. That is precisely why the international standard for casualty investigation - the Casualty Investigation Code, adopted by resolution MSC.255(84) on 16 May 2008 - is directed at establishing the circumstances and causes of a casualty so that safety may be enhanced, and is expressly not an exercise in apportioning blame.

The Human Element is the subject area. It is the recognition that people are an integral part of the maritime system, and it is the broadest of the three terms. The Organization treats it as a complex multi-dimensional issue affecting safety, security and protection of the marine environment, and - crucially - as involving the entire spectrum of human activity: ships' crews, shore-based management, regulatory bodies, recognized organizations, shipyards, legislators and others. That framing is set out in the IMO's Human Element Vision, Principles and Goals, resolution A.947(23).

It is therefore not confined to seafarers, and that is the commonest misunderstanding of the term. Its regulatory expression is the whole apparatus that deals with people: the ISM Code for safety management, resources and the master's authority; STCW for competence, training and fitness for duty; and MLC 2006 for hours of work and rest and for living and working conditions. Human Element answers the question 'who and what is in scope?'

Human Error is an event. It is a specific occasion on which a planned action fails to achieve its intended outcome, or on which the plan itself was inadequate. It is the narrowest of the three terms, it is retrospective, and it describes what happened, not why.
It is not a single thing, and distinguishing the types is worth marks because each has a different remedy:

ul: Skill-based slips and lapses - the intention was right and the execution failed. Operating the adjacent valve; omitting a step through interruption. Remedy: design and interruption management.
Rule-based mistakes - a good rule applied in the wrong situation, or a bad rule applied correctly. Remedy: better procedures and better diagnosis training.
Knowledge-based mistakes - a novel situation with no rule available, reasoned through incorrectly under time pressure. Remedy: training, decision support and expert access.

Violations - deliberate departures from a rule, which are not errors at all. They may be routine (the shortcut everyone uses), situational (the rule cannot be complied with in the conditions given) or exceptional. Remedy: find out why the rule is not workable, because a routine violation is a statement about the procedure, not about the person.

blocks.p: Human Factors is the scientific discipline, and its application. It is the study of the interaction between people, equipment, procedures, organisation and environment, and the use of that knowledge to design systems that fit the people who must operate them - rather than expecting people to adapt to whatever has been built.

It is the only one of the three that is proactive and prospective. Its subject matter is workload and attention, fatigue and circadian rhythm, the design of controls, displays and alarms, automation and mode awareness, anthropometry and the physical environment, procedure design, communication and team behaviour. Human Factors answers the question 'how do we study this, and what do we change?'

blocks.h: 7. (b) How the three differ, worked through one incident

blocks.p: The distinction is easiest to see on a single event. An engineer, at the end of a long watch, opens the wrong valve and floods a space.

rows: Human Element
The domain - the whole scope of human involvement, from the regulator to the rating
Everything that put him there: manning level, the company's schedule, rest-hour compliance, training given, the safety culture that decided whether he would report a near miss
Human Error
The outcome - the specific act that failed
He opened the wrong valve. A skill-based slip
Human Factors
The discipline - why the act happened, and what to change
Two identical valves, adjacent, unlabelled, poorly lit, operated at the end of a 6-on 6-off watch. The interface and the watch pattern made this error probable

blocks.p: So the three terms sit at different levels: Human Element is the field, Human Factors is the method, and Human Error is the event. Their relationship can be put in one sentence - Human Error is what you see; Human Factors is how you explain and prevent it; the Human Element is the whole territory in which both live.

The distinction is not academic, because each term implies a different response. Treat the flooding as human error alone and you issue a warning and add a line to a checklist, and the next engineer makes the same slip. Treat it as a human-factors problem and you label and re-site the valves, improve the lighting and review the watch pattern, and the error becomes difficult to make. Treat it as a human-element problem and you ask why the ship was manned and scheduled so that a fatigued engineer was working alone at that hour - which is the only level at which the condition can actually be removed.

The marks are printed 6 and 10. Limb (a) is a single focused demand: discuss the term 'human error' as referred to here - and the words 'of a complex hierarchical socio-technical system' are not decoration, they are the instruction. The examiner is telling you what frame to use. An answer that defines human error as a mistake made by a person, without engaging that phrase, cannot score well however fluent it is.

Limb (b) asks how three terms differ, with suitable examples. The word examples is printed and is the cheapest set of marks on the question. One worked incident that distinguishes all three - as at step 7 - is worth more than three separate definitions, because it demonstrates the distinction rather than asserting it.

blocks.h: The one idea that organises the whole question

blocks.p: Human error is a symptom, not a cause. It is the label an investigator applies at the point where he stops asking why.

Everything else follows. The 80 per cent figure is high because a person is present at the end of nearly every chain, not because people are unusually unreliable. The word hierarchical matters because the conditions for the error were set by people higher up the system and long before the event. And the three terms differ because they sit at three different levels of that same system - the event, the explanation, and the territory.

blocks.p: If you can write that table you have limb (b)'s first half. Then add one worked incident and the taxonomy of error types, and it is complete.

ul: Accepting the 80 per cent figure as a finding and building the answer on it. Limb (a) is asking you to examine the claim, not repeat it.
Ignoring the phrase 'complex hierarchical socio-technical system'. It is the examiner handing you the frame.
Using Human Element and Human Factors interchangeably. One is a domain, the other a discipline - which is precisely what limb (b) says people do wrongly.
Confining the Human Element to seafarers. The IMO's framing expressly includes shore management, regulators, recognized organizations, shipyards and legislators.
Treating violations as errors. A violation is deliberate. A routine violation is evidence that the procedure is unworkable, not that the person is careless.
Giving no examples in limb (b) when the stem prints the word.
Concluding that the answer to human error is more training and more care. That is the response the question is testing you against.
Naming a real casualty and misdescribing it. If you are not certain of the findings, use a constructed example instead.
Quoting an author, a model name or a study. Explain the mechanism instead - it scores the same and cannot be wrong.

Do you accept that 80 per cent of accidents are caused by human error? The expected answer is a qualified no - a human action can be identified in most causal chains, which is a different statement, and the figure reflects where investigations stop.
What does 'hierarchical' add? That the conditions for a sharp-end error are created by decisions taken higher in the system and earlier in time - manning, budget, schedule, design, procedures.

Give me an active failure and a latent condition from the same event. The engineer opening the wrong valve is the active failure; the unlabelled identical valves and the watch pattern are latent conditions.
Is a violation an error? No - it is deliberate. Ask instead why the rule is not being followed.
Which of the three terms is the widest? Human Element. Which is proactive? Human Factors. Which is retrospective? Human Error.

As Chief Engineer, your third engineer opens the wrong valve. What do you do? Establish why the act made sense to him at the time; then change the conditions - labelling, siting, lighting, watch pattern, workload - rather than issuing a warning.

Which instrument requires you to look beyond the last unsafe act? The Casualty Investigation Code, resolution MSC.255(84) of 16 May 2008, which is directed at circumstances and causes rather than at blame.

Where does the ISM Code fit? It is the regulatory expression of the human element at the organisational layer - resources and personnel, the master's overriding authority, and the reporting and analysis of non-conformities and hazardous occurrences.
Define human error in one sentence.
Define the human element.
What is ergonomics, and how does it relate to human factors?
Distinguish a slip from a mistake.
What is a latent condition? Give one from your own engine room.
Why is blaming the individual usually the wrong response?
What is a routine violation, and what does it tell you?
How does fatigue produce error rather than merely tiredness?
Name three human-factors interventions you could make on board this week.

blocks.p: Two limbs, seven steps. Limb (a) walks one argument: the figure is a stopping rule (1), the system is layered and the conditions come from above (2), so error is a symptom and not a cause (3). Limb (b) is three definitions and a demonstration: ELEMENT the domain (4), ERROR the event (5), FACTORS the discipline (6), then one incident that separates all three (7).

For the three terms use FIELD - METHOD - EVENT, and remember they get narrower in that order. For the error taxonomy use SLIP, LAPSE, MISTAKE, VIOLATION - and remember the last one is not an error at all.

For the worked example, keep one incident in your head and rehearse it in three registers: the wrong valve is the event; the identical unlabelled valves and the watch pattern are the factors; the manning, schedule and reporting culture are the element.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of what is claimed

blocks.p: This is a conceptual question and the answer is written as one. No instrument prescribes what these three terms mean, and none has been named to give the answer false authority. One instrument was read at source - resolution MSC.255(84) of 16 May 2008, adopting the Casualty Investigation Code - and it is used only for the proposition that the international standard for investigation is directed at circumstances and causes rather than blame.

Three limits are declared. IMO resolution A.947(23) is not held by MIW; it is cited by identity for the Organization's framing of the human element, with nothing quoted and no paragraph asserted. MIW holds no text-bearing copy of the ISM Code, STCW or MLC 2006, so all three are referred to at regime level only and no provision number is given. And the safety-science content is declared as established reference: no author is named and no publication, model name or case study is cited, because MIW holds none - the concepts are explained mechanistically instead, which scores identically and cannot be misattributed.

One point of substance about evidence. The 80 per cent figure is not endorsed anywhere in this answer. It is the examiner's printed premise, and limb (a) consists precisely of examining it. No alternative statistic is offered in its place - to replace one unverifiable figure with another would miss the point - and no named casualty is used. The worked example at step 7 is a constructed engine-room scenario, presented as an illustration and not as a report of a real incident.

On currency: this question carries no 2024 boundary at all. The concepts are long settled, nothing in the ISM, STCW or MLC regimes relevant to them moved during 2024, and the Casualty Investigation Code has been in force since 2010. Note only that the MLC 2022 amendments entered into force on 23 December 2024, after this sitting, and nothing in this answer depends on them.

Note in passing that the MLC 2022 amendments entered into force on 23 December 2024, AFTER this sitting, and that MSC.560(108) does not enter into force until 1 January 2026; neither is relied on.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW - the question is conceptual and international and asks for no statutory limb. No Indian provision is asserted, and the Merchant Shipping Act 2025, which commenced 15 March 2026, must not appear.
technical_ambiguities: 'Human error' in the printed statement is used loosely and the whole of limb (a) turns on that looseness. The answer distinguishes the popular usage - a careless individual - from the technical one - the last identifiable human action in a causal chain - and says which the statement actually supports.

'In your opinion' in limb (b) is a genuine invitation to take a position rather than hedge. The answer takes one: the three terms sit at different levels of the same system, and treating them as synonyms produces the wrong intervention.

'Suitable examples' could be answered with three unconnected illustrations. A single incident read in three registers is stronger, because it demonstrates that the terms describe different aspects of one situation rather than different situations.

Violations sit awkwardly inside a question about error. They are included because omitting them leaves the taxonomy incomplete and because the routine violation is the clearest evidence that a procedure rather than a person is at fault - but they are expressly labelled as NOT errors.
